items.name: Projectiles
path: Unit 1 Mechanics and Materials
Mechanics
S7 - how to make use of the independence of vertic
items.question: Two identical steel balls, P and Q, leave the edge of a horizontal table at the same instant. P is released from rest and falls vertically. Q is projected horizontally from the edge at 3.0 m s^-1. Air resistance is negligible. Which statement is correct? A: P lands first, because Q has further to travel; B: Q lands first, because it has the greater initial speed; C: P and Q land at the same time, and Q lands with the greater speed; D: P and Q land at the same time, and with the same speed.
items.answer: C: P and Q land at the same time, and Q lands with the greater speed
steps: The vertical and horizontal motions of a projectile are independent.
Both balls start with zero vertical velocity and have the same vertical acceleration g, so they fall the same height in the same time. A and B are wrong.
The vertical speed on landing is the same for both balls, but Q also keeps its horizontal speed of 3.0 m s^-1.
Speed on landing = sqrt(vx² + vy²), so Q lands with the greater speed. D is wrong, so the answer is C.

items.question: A ball is kicked from level ground at 20 m s⁻¹ at 30 degrees above the horizontal. Air resistance is negligible. What is the time between the kick and the ball returning to the ground? A: 1.0 s; B: 2.0 s; C: 3.5 s; D: 4.1 s.
steps: Take upwards as positive. The initial vertical velocity is uy = 20 sin 30 = 10 m s^-1.
The ball returns to the ground when its vertical displacement is zero: 0 = uy t - 0.5 g t², so t = 2 uy / g.
A has no factor 2 (time to the highest point only). C uses the horizontal component (cos 30) and D uses the whole speed 20 m s⁻¹ instead of the vertical component.

items.question: A stone is thrown at an angle above the horizontal. In practice the horizontal distance it travels before hitting the ground is less than the value calculated by ignoring air resistance. Explain why.
items.answer: Air resistance opposes the motion, so the horizontal velocity falls during the flight and the stone travels a shorter horizontal distance than the calculated range.
steps: Air resistance acts in the opposite direction to the stone's velocity throughout the flight
so the horizontal velocity decreases (it is not constant)
so the stone covers less horizontal distance in the flight, giving a range less than the calculated value
accept: While the stone rises, air resistance acts downwards as well as the weight, so the deceleration is greater than g and the maximum height is lower
The path is no longer a symmetrical parabola: the descent is steeper than the ascent
Some kinetic energy is transferred to thermal energy in the air, so the stone has less energy
Air resistance reduces the horizontal component of velocity continuously, unlike the ideal case

items.question: A stone is thrown from the top of a vertical cliff that is 45 m above the sea. It leaves the thrower's hand at 15 m s⁻¹ at 30 degrees above the horizontal. Ignore air resistance. A second stone is thrown from the same point at the same speed of 15 m s⁻¹, but horizontally. State and explain whether this stone hits the sea with a speed that is greater than, less than or equal to that of the first stone.
items.answer: Equal: same initial kinetic energy and the same fall of 45 m give the same final kinetic energy, so both hit the sea at 33.3 m s^-1.
steps: The speeds are equal
Both stones start with the same kinetic energy (same mass and same speed)
Both lose the same gravitational potential energy, m g h, in falling 45 m, so by conservation of energy the final kinetic energy, and hence the speed (v = sqrt(u² + 2gh) = 33.3 m s⁻¹), is the same
accept: Air resistance is negligible, so energy is conserved
The speed depends only on the initial speed and the vertical drop, not on the launch direction
Using components: the horizontal and vertical velocities differ for each stone, but the resultant speed at the sea is the same (33.3 m s⁻¹)

items.name: Graphs of motion
path: Unit 1 Mechanics and Materials
Mechanics
S2 - draw and interpret displacement-time, velocit
items.question: The displacement-time graph for a trolley moving along a straight track is a curve. Its gradient is positive at first, decreases steadily and becomes zero at t = 4.0 s. Which statement describes the motion of the trolley? A: it moves with constant velocity, then stops suddenly at 4.0 s; B: it speeds up steadily until 4.0 s; C: it returns to its starting point at 4.0 s; D: it slows down steadily and is momentarily at rest at 4.0 s.
items.answer: D: it slows down steadily and is momentarily at rest at 4.0 s
steps: The gradient of a displacement-time graph is the velocity.
A positive gradient that decreases steadily means the velocity is positive and falling steadily, so the trolley decelerates.
A zero gradient at 4.0 s means the velocity is zero at that instant, so the trolley is momentarily at rest.
A would give a straight line then a flat line; B needs an increasing gradient; C needs the displacement to fall back to zero, which needs a negative gradient. The answer is D.

items.question: The velocity-time graph for a lift moving upwards consists of three straight sections: the velocity rises from 0 to 4.0 m s⁻¹ in 2.0 s, stays at 4.0 m s⁻¹ for 6.0 s, then falls to zero in 3.0 s. What is the total distance travelled by the lift? A: 24 m; B: 28 m; C: 34 m; D: 44 m.
steps: The distance is the total area under the velocity-time graph.
Rising section: 0.5 x 2.0 x 4.0 = 4.0 m. Constant section: 6.0 x 4.0 = 24 m. Falling section: 0.5 x 3.0 x 4.0 = 6.0 m.
Total = 4.0 + 24 + 6.0 = 34 m, which is C.
A counts only the constant-velocity section, B leaves out the final triangle, and D treats the whole 11 s as if the lift moved at 4.0 m s⁻¹ (11 x 4.0 = 44 m).

items.question: A ball is released from rest above a hard floor, hits the floor and rebounds to a smaller height. Take upwards as positive and ignore air resistance. Describe the velocity-time graph for the motion from release until the ball reaches the top of its first bounce.
items.answer: A straight line of gradient -9.81 m s⁻² down to a negative velocity at impact, a near-vertical jump to a smaller positive velocity, then a parallel straight line falling to zero at the top of the bounce.
steps: Straight line starting at the origin and sloping downwards with gradient -9.81 m s⁻² (velocity becomes more negative at a constant rate)
The line reaches its most negative velocity at the instant of impact
Near-vertical line at the impact up to a positive velocity of smaller magnitude (the ball loses kinetic energy in the collision)
Straight line of the same gradient, -9.81 m s⁻² (parallel to the first line), falling to zero velocity at the top of the bounce
accept: The contact time is very short, so the change of velocity is almost instantaneous
The area enclosed by the second section is smaller than that of the first, because the rebound height is smaller than the release height
The line crosses the time axis at the top of the bounce with no change in gradient
Acceleration is constant at -9.81 m s⁻² whenever the ball is in the air, so the gradient is the same before and after the bounce

path: Unit 1 Mechanics and Materials

items.question: A car slows down uniformly from 24 m s⁻¹ to 8.0 m s⁻¹ while travelling 80 m along a straight road. What is the magnitude of its deceleration? A: 1.6 m s⁻²; B: 3.2 m s⁻²; C: 4.8 m s⁻²; D: 6.4 m s^-2.
steps: Use v² = u² + 2as with u = 24 m s⁻¹, v = 8.0 m s⁻¹ and s = 80 m.
a = (v² - u²) / (2s) = (64 - 576) / 160 = -3.2 m s⁻², so the deceleration is 3.2 m s⁻² (B).
A comes from using t = s / v (80 / 8.0 = 10 s); C comes from using t = s / u (3.3 s); D is (u² - v²) / s, which leaves out the factor 2.

items.question: A stone is released from rest and falls freely. It falls a distance d in the first interval of time t. What distance does it fall in the next interval of time t? Ignore air resistance. A: 3d; B: d; C: 4d; D: 2d.
steps: From rest, s = 0.5 g t², so the distance fallen is proportional to t^2.
In the first interval t the stone falls d. After 2t it has fallen (2)² d = 4d in total.
The distance fallen in the next interval = 4d - d = 3d, which is A.
B assumes constant speed, C is the total distance after 2t, and D assumes the distance is proportional to time.

items.question: A hammer and a feather are released together from the same height on the surface of the Moon. They hit the surface at the same time. Explain this observation.
items.answer: There is no air on the Moon, so the only force on each object is its weight and a = mg/m = g for both.
steps: The Moon has no atmosphere, so there is no air resistance on either object
The only force on each object is its weight, W = m g
a = F / m = m g / m = g, so the mass cancels: both fall with the same acceleration and land together
accept: Both start from rest and fall the same height with the same acceleration, so they take the same time
The gravitational field strength is the same at the same height for both objects
On Earth the feather would be slowed far more by air resistance than the hammer

items.answer: New time = 7.12 s, which is 1.5 times the original time, so the prediction is not correct.

Original time = 4.61 s, so the ratio = 7.12 / 4.61 = 1.5, not 2.

accept: The time to reach the highest point does double (1.53 s to 3.06 s) but the longer fall back down is not simply doubled

items.question: Two forces of magnitude 5.0 N and 12 N act at the same point. Which of the following could not be the magnitude of their resultant? A: 7.0 N; B: 13 N; C: 17 N; D: 18 N.
steps: The resultant is largest when the forces act in the same direction: 5.0 + 12 = 17 N.
It is smallest when they act in opposite directions: 12 - 5.0 = 7.0 N.
For any other angle the resultant lies between 7.0 N and 17 N (13 N at right angles, since sqrt(5.0² + 12²) = 13).
18 N is greater than the maximum of 17 N, so the answer is D.

items.question: A boat can travel at 3.0 m s⁻¹ in still water. It is steered directly across a river that flows at 1.2 m s⁻¹ parallel to its banks. What is the speed of the boat relative to the bank? A: 1.8 m s⁻¹; B: 2.7 m s⁻¹; C: 3.2 m s⁻¹; D: 4.2 m s^-1.
steps: The velocity of the boat relative to the water (3.0 m s⁻¹ across) and the velocity of the river (1.2 m s⁻¹ along the bank) are at right angles.
Speed relative to the bank = sqrt(3.0² + 1.2²) = sqrt(10.44) = 3.23 m s⁻¹ = 3.2 m s⁻¹ (C).
A subtracts the speeds (3.0 - 1.2), D adds them, and B uses sqrt(3.0² - 1.2²), which would apply to a different triangle.

items.answer: Ground speed = 211 m s⁻¹ on a bearing of 007 degrees (6.8 degrees east of north)
steps: The velocity of the aircraft relative to the air (north) and the wind velocity (east) are at right angles.
Ground speed = sqrt(210² + 25²) = sqrt(44725) = 211.5 m s⁻¹ = 211 m s^-1.
Angle east of north: tan(theta) = 25 / 210, so theta = 6.79 degrees.

items.answer: Horizontal component 38 N; vertical component 24 N; the vertical component reduces the normal contact force by 24 N.

items.question: Rain falls vertically at 9.0 m s⁻¹ relative to the ground. A train travels horizontally at 22 m s^-1. Explain why a passenger sees the raindrops moving at an angle to the vertical, and calculate this angle.
items.answer: The passenger measures velocities relative to the moving train, so the rain has a horizontal component of 22 m s⁻¹ backwards as well as 9.0 m s⁻¹ downwards; angle to the vertical = 68 degrees.
steps: tan(theta) = horizontal component / vertical component = 22 / 9.0.
theta = 67.8 degrees = 68 degrees to the vertical.
Velocity of the rain relative to the passenger = velocity of the rain relative to the ground minus the velocity of the train.
Relative to the train the rain therefore has a horizontal component of 22 m s⁻¹ towards the back of the train as well as 9.0 m s⁻¹ downwards, so its path is slanted.
accept: Relative velocity: the passenger is in a frame moving forwards at 22 m s⁻¹, so everything outside appears to move backwards at 22 m s⁻¹
The rain's speed relative to the train is sqrt(22² + 9.0²) = 24 m s⁻¹
The angle to the horizontal is 22 degrees (90 - 68)

items.question: A book rests on a horizontal table. Which pair of forces is a Newton's third law pair? A: the weight of the book and the upward force of the table on the book; B: the weight of the book and the downward force of the book on the table; C: the upward force of the table on the book and the weight of the table; D: the upward force of the table on the book and the downward force of the book on the table.
items.answer: D: the upward force of the table on the book and the downward force of the book on the table
steps: A Newton's third law pair consists of two forces of the same type, equal in size and opposite in direction, that act on two different bodies and arise from the same interaction.
The table pushes up on the book (a contact force) and the book pushes down on the table (a contact force): same type, equal and opposite, on different bodies. This is D.
A is wrong: both forces act on the book and they balance each other, which is the first law, not the third. They are also different types of force.
B is wrong because the weight is a gravitational force, so its third-law partner is the book's pull on the Earth. C involves the table's weight, which is not part of the same interaction.

items.question: State Newton's third law of motion and explain why the two forces in a third-law pair do not cancel each other out.
items.answer: If A exerts a force on B, B exerts an equal and opposite force of the same type on A; the forces act on different bodies, so they cannot cancel.
steps: When body A exerts a force on body B, B exerts a force on A (the two forces form an interaction pair)
The two forces are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction
The forces act on different bodies, and forces cancel only if they act on the same body, so they cannot cancel
accept: The two forces are of the same type (for example both gravitational or both contact forces)
The two forces exist at the same time and one cannot exist without the other
Example: the Earth pulls on a book and the book pulls on the Earth with equal and opposite forces
A resultant is found only by adding forces that act on one body

steps: The box is in equilibrium, so the resultant force on it is zero.

items.question: Explain why the braking distance of a car is longer on a wet road than on a dry road when the car brakes from the same initial speed.
items.answer: Less friction on a wet road gives a smaller maximum braking force and deceleration, so the braking distance s = u² / (2a) is longer.
steps: The braking force on the car is the frictional force between the tyres and the road
Water reduces the maximum friction, so the braking force is smaller and the deceleration (a = F / m) is smaller
For the same initial speed s = u² / (2a), so a smaller deceleration gives a longer braking distance

The same kinetic energy must be removed by work done against friction (W = F s), so a smaller force needs a longer distance

items.question: Two trolleys collide on a horizontal track and friction is negligible. The collision is inelastic. Which statement about the total momentum and the total kinetic energy of the trolleys is correct? A: the total momentum decreases and the total kinetic energy decreases; B: the total momentum is conserved and the total kinetic energy is conserved; C: the total momentum decreases and the total kinetic energy is conserved; D: the total momentum is conserved and the total kinetic energy decreases.
items.answer: D: the total momentum is conserved and the total kinetic energy decreases
steps: Momentum is conserved in every collision when no external resultant force acts. Friction is negligible, so the total momentum is conserved.
In an inelastic collision some kinetic energy is transferred to other forms (thermal energy, sound, deformation), so the total kinetic energy decreases.
This is D. A and C wrongly say momentum decreases; B describes an elastic collision.

items.answer: Gravitational potential energy goes to kinetic energy, then to elastic energy and back to kinetic energy at the impact, but some energy is dissipated as thermal energy and sound, so the ball rises to a lower height.

steps: For an ideal gas the mean translational kinetic energy of a particle is 0.5 m <c²> = 1.5 k T, which depends only on the temperature.

items.answer: When submerged the upthrust (rho_liquid V g) is greater than the weight (rho_object V g), so there is a resultant upward force. At the surface the displaced volume falls until the upthrust equals the weight, so the resultant force is zero.
steps: Upthrust (weight of liquid displaced, rho_liquid V g) is greater than the weight of the object (rho_object V g) when it is fully submerged, because rho_object < rho_liquid and the volume V is the same.
So the resultant force is upwards and the object accelerates upwards to the surface.
At the surface the volume of liquid displaced falls until the upthrust equals the weight, so the resultant force is zero and the object floats at rest.
accept: Compares upthrust per unit volume (rho_liquid g) with weight per unit volume (rho_object g).
Part of the object is above the surface when it floats at rest.
No resultant force at the surface, so no acceleration (Newton's first law).

items.question: Describe the difference between laminar flow and turbulent flow of a fluid past an object.
items.answer: Laminar: layers of fluid slide smoothly past each other along steady, parallel streamlines with no mixing. Turbulent: the flow is irregular and swirling (eddies), with mixing between layers and a velocity at a point that fluctuates.
steps: Laminar flow: layers of fluid slide smoothly past one another along steady, parallel streamlines, with no mixing.
Turbulent flow: irregular, swirling flow with eddies and mixing, so the velocity at a point changes unpredictably with time.
accept: Laminar: the velocity at any point in the fluid stays constant with time.

items.answer: The diameter contributes most (3.3% since d is squared). Total percentage uncertainty in E = 5.7%.
steps: Percentage uncertainties: diameter 0.005 / 0.300 x 100 = 1.7%; length 0.010 / 2.50 x 100 = 0.4%; gradient 2.0%.

items.answer: The wave travelling along the string reflects at the fixed ends. The incident and reflected waves (same frequency and amplitude) travelling in opposite directions superpose to give nodes and antinodes.
steps: The wave travelling along the string is reflected at the fixed ends.

At nodes the waves are always in antiphase (destructive interference, no movement); at antinodes they are in phase (constructive interference, maximum amplitude), giving a pattern that does not travel along the string.
accept: There is a node at each fixed end.
Adjacent nodes are half a wavelength apart.
A stationary wave does not transfer energy along the string.

items.answer: Light is a transverse wave. The first filter passes only oscillations in one plane; the second passes none of this light when its transmission direction is at 90 degrees to the first, so the light must be plane polarised, which only transverse waves can be.

steps: Grating spacing d = 1 / (300 × 10³) = 3.33 × 10⁻⁶ m, and tan theta = 0.398 / 2.00 gives theta = 11.25 degrees (use the unrounded angle: 11 degrees would give 636 nm).
n lambda = d sin theta with n = 1, so lambda = 3.33 × 10⁻⁶ x sin(11.25 degrees) = 3.33 × 10⁻⁶ x 0.1952.
lambda = 6.51 × 10⁻⁷ m, i.e. 651 nm.

items.question: Light of frequency below the threshold frequency of a zinc plate does not cause photoelectric emission, however intense the light is. Explain this observation using the photon model of light.
items.answer: Each electron absorbs a single photon of energy hf. If hf is less than the work function no electron gains enough energy to escape, and a greater intensity only gives more photons per second, not more energy per photon.
steps: Light consists of photons, each with energy E = h f, and one electron interacts with one photon.
Below the threshold frequency the photon energy is less than the work function (h f < phi), so an electron cannot escape from the surface.
Increasing the intensity only increases the number of photons per second, not the energy of each photon, and electrons cannot build up energy from several photons, so there is still no emission.
accept: Wave theory predicts that energy would build up over time and release electrons, which is not observed.
No emission occurs even after a long exposure time.
The work function is the minimum energy needed to remove an electron from the surface.

items.answer: A greater current heats the filament, so the metal ions vibrate with a larger amplitude. The electrons collide with the ions more often, so for a given p.d. their drift velocity and the current are smaller, and the resistance V / I is greater.
steps: A greater current heats the filament, so its temperature rises and the metal ions vibrate with greater amplitude.

accept: The number of free electrons per unit volume in a metal stays approximately constant, so the change is due to the collisions.

items.question: Explain why the terminal potential difference of a battery decreases as the current drawn from the battery increases.
items.answer: The battery has internal resistance r. The terminal p.d. is V = E - I r, where E is constant, so a larger current gives a larger p.d. lost across the internal resistance and a smaller terminal p.d.

items.answer: Original: 75% delivered to the external circuit. With the 5.0 ohm resistor it is 82%, so the student is correct.

steps: The moving rod changes the flux linkage with the circuit, so an e.m.f. is induced and a current flows in the circuit.

items.answer: The alternating current produces a changing magnetic flux in the core, which links the secondary coil, so the flux linkage in the secondary changes and an e.m.f. is induced (Faraday's law). A steady direct current gives a constant flux, so there is no change of flux linkage and no e.m.f.
steps: The alternating current in the primary coil produces a magnetic flux that changes continuously.
The soft iron core links this flux with the secondary coil, so the flux linkage in the secondary changes continuously.
By Faraday's law an e.m.f. proportional to the rate of change of flux linkage is induced in the secondary coil.
A steady direct current gives a constant flux, so there is no change of flux linkage and no e.m.f. is induced.
accept: The iron core concentrates the flux so that nearly all of it links both coils.
Lenz's law gives the direction of the induced e.m.f.

items.question: Explain why a star of much greater mass than the Sun ends its life in a supernova, whereas a star of similar mass to the Sun does not.
items.answer: A massive star fuses elements up to iron, then its core collapses in a supernova; a Sun-like star becomes a white dwarf.
steps: In a very massive star gravity compresses the core to a much higher temperature, so successive fusion stages build heavier elements, up to iron
Iron has the highest binding energy per nucleon, so fusing iron absorbs energy rather than releasing it and the outward pressure from fusion stops
The core then collapses under gravity and the outer layers are thrown off in a supernova, leaving a neutron star or black hole
In a Sun-like star the core never becomes hot enough for the later stages of fusion; it expels its outer layers as a planetary nebula and the core remains as a white dwarf
accept: More massive stars have a greater gravitational pressure, so they reach higher core temperatures
A massive star fuses hydrogen much faster and so has a shorter life on the main sequence
The remnant becomes a neutron star or a black hole depending on the mass of the core
The star becomes a red supergiant, rather than a red giant, before the supernova

items.question: The spectral lines in the light from distant galaxies are shifted towards longer wavelengths, and the shift is greater for galaxies that are further away. Explain what these observations suggest about the universe.
items.answer: Galaxies recede faster the further away they are: the universe is expanding from an earlier hot, dense state.
steps: The longer observed wavelengths are a Doppler (red) shift, so the galaxies are receding from the Earth
The greater redshift of more distant galaxies shows that recession speed increases with distance (v proportional to d), as in a uniformly expanding universe
Tracing the expansion back in time, everything was once much closer together, supporting a Big Bang origin
accept: Space itself is expanding, so the wavelength of light is stretched as it travels

Hubble's law v = H0 d describes the relationship
The expansion can be used to estimate the age of the universe as 1 / H0

items.answer: Uniform 2.7 K black-body radiation from all directions: the stretched remnant of the hot early universe.
steps: The radiation is detected from all directions with almost the same intensity, and has a black-body spectrum corresponding to a temperature of about 2.7 K
The Big Bang model predicts that the early universe was very hot and dense and filled with high-energy radiation, which should still be present as a background
As space expanded the wavelengths of this radiation were stretched (redshifted) into the microwave region, matching the observed spectrum

The temperature of the radiation has fallen as the universe expanded
The peak wavelength of about 1 mm corresponds to a 2.7 K black body (Wien's law)

items.answer: D: timing 40 oscillations and dividing the time by 40

steps: The gradient = -1 / (RC), so RC = 1 / 0.0265.
RC = 37.74 s, which is 37.7 s.

items.question: The capacitor is labelled 1000 microfarad with a tolerance of +/- 10%. The student calculates that the capacitance is 803 microfarad, using a gradient of (-0.0265 +/- 0.0013) s^-1. Evaluate whether her result is consistent with the label, and suggest one reason for any difference.
items.answer: Not consistent: 765 to 844 microfarad does not overlap 900 to 1100 microfarad; e.g. leakage current.
steps: The labelled range is 1000 +/- 10% = 900 to 1100 microfarad
The gradient range 0.0252 to 0.0278 s⁻¹ gives RC from 36.0 s to 39.7 s, so C from 765 to 844 microfarad
This range does not overlap 900 to 1100 microfarad, so the result is not consistent with the label
A possible reason: a leakage current through the capacitor (or a parallel voltmeter) lets charge escape faster, so the measured time constant is too small
accept: The resistor's actual resistance differs from its marked 47 kilohm (resistor tolerance), so C = RC / R is wrong
Electrolytic capacitors often have a wide tolerance, so the label value may not apply within +/- 10%
Errors in timing (reaction time) or in reading V would affect the gradient
The capacitance may have changed with age or temperature, so the true value is no longer within the labelled tolerance

items.question: A nucleus of iodine-131 contains 53 protons. Which of the following gives the number of neutrons and the number of nucleons in this nucleus? 78 neutrons; 131 nucleons 53 neutrons; 131 nucleons 78 neutrons; 184 nucleons 131 neutrons; 78 nucleons
items.ms: The nucleon number is 131 (protons + neutrons), so the number of neutrons is 131 − 53 = 78. B gives the proton number as the number of neutrons. C adds the proton number to the nucleon number. D swaps the neutron number and the nucleon number.
items.why: S111 has come up in 12 of 19 sessions, almost always as a one-mark 'how many neutrons' MCQ (Jan2024, Oct2025, Jan2026, Jun2026); swapped and added numbers are the standard distractors.

items.ms: ⁵⁶₂₆Fe has 56 − 26 = 30 neutrons, and ⁵⁸₂₈Ni has 58 − 28 = 30 neutrons. A has the same nucleon number but only 29 neutrons. B is another isotope of iron, with the same number of protons but 31 neutrons. D has a nucleon number of 30, but only 16 neutrons.

items.question: In 1919, Rutherford directed alpha particles into nitrogen gas. Occasionally an alpha particle was absorbed by a nitrogen nucleus. A nucleus of oxygen and a fast-moving particle X were produced. The equation for this reaction is ⁴₂He + ¹⁴₇N → ¹⁷₈O + X Deduce the nucleon number and the proton number of X, and name particle X. Oxygen-16 is the most common isotope of oxygen. Compare a nucleus of oxygen-17 with a nucleus of oxygen-16. In 1932, Chadwick showed that nuclei also contain neutrons. Suggest why the earlier alpha-particle scattering experiments gave no evidence that the nucleus contains neutrons.
items.ms: Nucleon number of X = (4 + 14 − 17) = 1 and proton number of X = (2 + 7 − 8) = 1 X is a proton Both nuclei contain 8 protons / have the same proton number Oxygen-17 has 9 neutrons and oxygen-16 has 8 neutrons / oxygen-17 has one more neutron Neutrons are uncharged, so they exert no electrostatic force on the alpha particles / the deflection of the alpha particles depends only on the (positive) charge of the nucleus
items.why: S111 has come up in 12 of 19 sessions; the only structured part (Jun2024 Q11(a)) completed a reaction equation, and Jan2026 Q7 tested that alpha scattering could not show neutrons, so both ideas are combined here in a new historical reaction.

items.question: In the alpha-particle scattering experiment, a beam of alpha particles was directed at a thin gold foil. Which observation shows that most of the mass of an atom is concentrated in a very small volume? Most alpha particles passed straight through the foil. Some alpha particles were deflected through small angles. The number of alpha particles detected each minute was about the same at all angles. A very small fraction of the alpha particles were deflected through more than 90°.
items.ms: Turning an alpha particle back needs a very large force from a very small, massive (and charged) region, the nucleus. A shows that the atom is mostly empty space. B on its own could be explained by charge spread through the atom. C was not observed: the number detected fell rapidly as the angle increased.
items.why: S112 has come up in 18 of 19 sessions, with a 'which conclusion' MCQ in most of them (Oct2024, Jan2025, Oct2025, Jan2026); here the student must match a conclusion to its observation instead.

items.question: The alpha-particle scattering experiment is repeated with the same gold foil, but the alpha particles now have a greater initial kinetic energy. Which of the following describes the change in the number of alpha particles deflected through more than 90° and the change in the distance of closest approach of an alpha particle travelling directly towards a nucleus? number deflected through more than 90° decreases; distance of closest approach decreases number deflected through more than 90° decreases; distance of closest approach increases number deflected through more than 90° increases; distance of closest approach decreases number deflected through more than 90° increases; distance of closest approach increases
items.ms: A faster alpha particle has more kinetic energy to transfer to electric potential energy, so it gets closer before stopping (Ek = kQq/r, so r is smaller). It also spends less time near any nucleus, so it must pass much closer to a nucleus to be turned through a large angle: fewer are deflected through more than 90°. B reverses the closest-approach change. C and D assume that more energy means more large-angle deflections.
items.why: Alpha-scattering MCQs (Oct2024, Jan2025, Jun2025, Jan2026) have never asked how the results change with the energy of the alpha particles, which links S112 to the closest-approach calculations of S98.

items.question: The diagram shows the path of an alpha particle as it passes close to a gold nucleus. Which arrow shows the direction of the resultant force on the alpha particle at point P? arrow A arrow B arrow C arrow D
items.ms: The force is the electrostatic repulsion between the two positive charges, so it acts along the line from the nucleus through P, away from the nucleus (B). A would be an attraction. C is the direction of the velocity, not the force. D is perpendicular to the velocity, which would be true for a magnetic force, not for the electric force from a point charge.
items.why: Jan2024 Q10 and Jan2025 Q5 asked about alpha paths near a nucleus; the direction of the force along the path is the step behind both and has not been asked directly.

items.question: The diagram shows apparatus used to repeat the alpha-particle scattering experiment. A narrow beam of alpha particles is directed at a thin gold foil in an evacuated chamber. A detector can be moved around the foil to count the alpha particles scattered through any angle θ. Before this experiment, many scientists accepted the 'plum pudding' model of the atom, in which the positive charge and the mass are spread evenly throughout the atom, with electrons embedded in it. Describe the results that are obtained as the detector is moved from θ = 0° to θ = 180°, and explain how these results led to the plum pudding model being replaced by the nuclear model of the atom.
items.ms: IC1 Most alpha particles are detected at θ = 0° / pass straight through the foil undeflected IC2 So most of the atom is empty space IC3 The number detected decreases as θ increases; some are deflected through small angles IC4 A very small number are detected at θ greater than 90° / some come straight back IC5 So (most of) the mass and the positive charge are concentrated in a very small volume, the nucleus, which repels the alpha particles strongly IC6 In the plum pudding model the charge and mass are spread out, so the forces are too small to deflect alpha particles through large angles; only the nuclear model explains the results
items.why: Alpha-scattering 6-mark answers came up in Jan2020, Oct2021, Oct2025 and Jun2026; tying each observation to a detector angle and to the plum pudding model covers the 'how our understanding has changed' half of the spec point.

items.question: The nuclear model describes an atom as a very small nucleus surrounded by electrons. The radius of a gold atom is 1.44 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. The radius of a nucleus of gold-197 is 7.0 × 10⁻¹⁵ m. Calculate the ratio volume of a gold atom / volume of its nucleus. The mass of a nucleon is about 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg. Show that the density of a gold-197 nucleus is about 2 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³. The density of gold metal is 1.93 × 10⁴ kg m⁻³. Explain what the comparison of this value with the density of the nucleus shows about the structure of a gold atom. Suggest why the electrons in the gold atoms have almost no effect on the paths of the alpha particles in the scattering experiment.
items.ms: Use of V = 4/3 πr³ / ratio of radii cubed ratio = 8.7 × 10¹² Mass of nucleus = 197 × 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg (= 3.29 × 10⁻²⁵ kg) Use of ρ = m/V with V = 4/3 πr³ ρ = 2.29 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³ The nucleus is about 10¹³ times as dense as the metal (ratio ≈ 1 × 10¹³) So almost all of the mass of the atom is in the nucleus, which takes up only a tiny fraction of the atom's volume; the rest of the atom is mostly empty space An electron's mass is very small compared with an alpha particle's (about 1/7300), so a collision with an electron hardly changes the alpha particle's momentum
items.why: S112's spec includes 'how our understanding of atomic structure has changed'; the size and density of the nucleus lie behind every 'mass concentrated in a small volume' marking point but have not been asked as a calculation.

items.question: In an alpha-particle scattering experiment, alpha particles of kinetic energy 5.5 MeV are directed at a thin gold foil in an evacuated chamber. The proton number of gold is 79. The diagram shows the paths of two alpha particles, P and Q, as they pass close to the same gold nucleus. The dashed line R shows the initial path of a third alpha particle. Explain why the gold foil must be very thin. Explain why alpha particle Q is deflected through a larger angle than alpha particle P. Complete the diagram to show the path of alpha particle R as it passes the nucleus. Another alpha particle of kinetic energy 5.5 MeV travels directly towards the centre of a gold nucleus. The nucleus may be treated as a point charge. Show that the distance of closest approach is about 4 × 10⁻¹⁴ m. Calculate the electrostatic force on the alpha particle at its point of closest approach. A student says that the calculation in (d)(i) shows that the radius of a gold nucleus is about 4 × 10⁻¹⁴ m. Comment on the student's statement. The gold foil is replaced by an aluminium foil with the same number of atoms per unit area. The proton number of aluminium is 13. Explain how the number of alpha particles deflected through more than 90° would change.
items.ms: Alpha particles are strongly ionising / have a short range, so they would be absorbed (stopped) by a thick foil So that each alpha particle is deflected by only one nucleus / there are no multiple deflections So that the alpha particles have (almost) their initial kinetic energy when they reach a nucleus Q passes closer to the nucleus so the (electrostatic) repulsive force on Q is larger (F ∝ 1/r²) Smooth curve deflected away from the nucleus (upwards), with no sharp change of direction Deflection greater than that of P but less than that of Q Conversion of 5.5 MeV to J (8.8 × 10⁻¹³ J) Use of Ek = kQq/r (or Ek = qV with V = Q/4πε₀r), with Q = 79e and q = 2e r = 4.13 × 10⁻¹⁴ m Use of F = kQq/r² F = 21 N The alpha particle is stopped and turned back by the repulsion before it reaches (touches) the nucleus So the radius of the nucleus is less than 4 × 10⁻¹⁴ m; the value is only an upper limit Fewer alpha particles are deflected through more than 90° An aluminium nucleus has a smaller charge (13e compared with 79e) so the repulsive force at a given distance is smaller / an alpha particle must pass much closer to a nucleus to be deflected through a large angle An aluminium nucleus has a smaller mass, so it recoils more (and turns the alpha particle back less easily)
items.why: S112 has come up in 18 of 19 sessions; thin-foil reasons (Oct2021 Q13(b)) and closest-approach estimates recur, but the effect of a foil with a smaller nuclear charge and what the closest approach really tells us have never been asked.

items.question: In an electron gun, a current in a filament heats it and electrons are released. The electrons are then accelerated by a potential difference between the filament and the anode. The current in the filament is increased. The accelerating potential difference does not change. Which of the following describes the effect on the number of electrons released per second and on the speed of the electrons leaving the anode? number released per second unchanged; speed increases number released per second increases; speed increases number released per second increases; speed unchanged number released per second unchanged; speed unchanged
items.ms: A larger current makes the filament hotter, so more electrons gain enough energy to escape (thermionic emission). Each electron still gains Ek = eV from the same accelerating p.d., so the speed is unchanged. A and B link the filament current to the speed. D ignores the higher filament temperature.
items.why: Thermionic emission MCQs come up almost every session (Jun2023 to Jun2026); Jan2026 Q6 asked how to increase the current in a vacuum diode, so separating the number of electrons from their speed is a likely next step.

items.question: The diagram shows an electron deflection tube. Electrons are released from a heated cathode and accelerated by a potential difference of 3.0 kV between the cathode and the anode. The electron beam then passes between two horizontal parallel plates. The plates are 4.0 cm apart and the potential difference between them is 1.2 kV. A uniform magnetic field, directed into the page, acts in the region between the plates. Show that the speed of the electrons leaving the anode is about 3 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹. The magnetic flux density is adjusted until the beam passes between the plates without being deflected. Explain why the beam is not deflected. Calculate the magnetic flux density needed for the beam to pass undeflected. The accelerating potential difference is now increased. The potential difference between the plates and the magnetic flux density do not change. State and explain the effect on the path of the beam between the plates.
items.ms: Use of W = QV (Ek = eV) Use of Ek = ½mv² v = 3.25 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹ The electric force (eE) on each electron is upwards (towards the positive plate) and the magnetic force (Bev) is downwards The two forces are equal in size, so the resultant force on each electron is zero (no acceleration perpendicular to the beam) Use of E = V/d Use of eE = Bev (B = E/v) B = 9.2 × 10⁻⁴ T The beam is deflected downwards (towards the negative plate), because the magnetic force (Bev) increases with speed but the electric force (eE) does not

items.question: A linear accelerator (linac) uses an alternating potential difference of frequency 25 MHz. A proton travels through one of the drift tubes at a constant speed of 4.0 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹. What is the length of this drift tube? 0.040 m 0.080 m 0.16 m 80 m
items.ms: The p.d. must reverse while the proton is inside the tube, so the time in the tube is half a period: t = 1/(2f) = 2.0 × 10⁻⁸ s, and L = vt = 0.080 m. A uses a quarter of a period. C uses a whole period. D takes 25 MHz as 25 kHz.
items.why: Linac questions recur (Jun2022 Q13, Jun2024 Q16(b), Oct2024 Q16(b), Jan2026 Q8 MCQ); the half-period timing behind 'the tubes get longer' has not been asked as a calculation.

items.question: A cyclotron accelerates alpha particles using an alternating potential difference of frequency 9.0 MHz. The cyclotron is then used to accelerate protons. The magnetic flux density is unchanged. What frequency of alternating potential difference is now needed? 4.5 MHz 9.0 MHz 18 MHz 36 MHz
items.ms: f = BQ/2πm. For a proton Q is halved and m is about a quarter of the alpha particle's, so f = 9.0 MHz × (6.64/1.67) ÷ 2 = 18 MHz. A inverts the ratio. B assumes the frequency does not depend on the particle. D allows for the mass but not the charge.
items.why: Cyclotron frequency MCQs came up in Oct2025 Q8 and Jun2026 Q5; changing the particle (charge and mass together) is the untested angle on f = BQ/2πm.

items.question: Which statement about a proton being accelerated in a cyclotron is correct? The magnetic force on the proton does no work on it. The magnetic field increases the speed of the proton while it is inside a dee. The electric field inside each dee makes the proton move in a semicircle. The time the proton takes to travel round each dee increases as its speed increases.
items.ms: The magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it changes the direction but does no work and the speed is constant inside a dee. B: only the electric field in the gap increases the speed. C: there is no electric field inside the dees; the magnetic force gives the semicircle. D: T = 2πm/BQ does not depend on the speed, because the radius increases in proportion to the speed.
items.why: Examiner reports (Jun2024, Jan2025) single out 'acceleration by the magnetic field' and not saying where the electric field is as the commonest cyclotron errors; S114 has come up in 18 of 19 sessions.

items.question: Particle detectors at the Large Hadron Collider record the tracks of charged particles produced in collisions. The detector is in a strong uniform magnetic field. items.question: A linear accelerator (linac) accelerates protons. It consists of a line of metal drift tubes in an evacuated chamber. Alternate tubes are connected to opposite terminals of an alternating potential difference of constant frequency f = 15 MHz, as shown. Protons start from rest at the source. A proton crosses a gap before it enters each tube, so a proton in tube n has crossed n gaps. The potential difference across a gap is at its peak value V₀ each time a proton crosses it. Explain why the drift tubes must get longer along the linac. Show that the length L of tube n is given by L² = (eV₀ / 2mf²) n where m is the mass of a proton. The table gives the lengths of the first six drift tubes. Plot a graph of L² against n on the grid. Use the third column of the table for your processed data. Use your graph to determine V₀.
items.ms: The time spent in each tube must be the same: half the period of the alternating p.d. (so that the p.d. has reversed when the proton reaches the next gap) The speed of the protons increases after each gap, so the tubes must be longer to keep the time the same (s = vt) Kinetic energy of a proton in tube n = neV₀ ½mv² = neV₀, so v² = 2neV₀/m Time in tube = 1/(2f), so L = v/(2f) and L² = v²/4f² = (eV₀/2mf²) n L² values correct (to 3 s.f.) Axes labelled with quantities and units, and sensible scales (points cover at least half the grid) All points plotted accurately (to within half a small square) Best-fit straight line (through the origin) Gradient calculated using a large triangle Use of gradient = eV₀/2mf² V₀ = 1.5 × 10⁵ V
items.why: Linac explanations recur (Oct2020, Jun2022, Jun2024, Oct2024, Oct2025 Q13 asked why the tubes lengthen); analysing the tube lengths with a straight-line graph has never been asked and tests the same idea through data.

items.question: Hospitals use cyclotrons to accelerate protons, which are then used to make radioactive isotopes for medical imaging. The diagram shows a cyclotron viewed from above. The two dees are in a uniform magnetic field directed into the page. An alternating potential difference is applied between the dees. Explain how the cyclotron increases the kinetic energy of the protons, and why the frequency of the alternating potential difference can stay constant as the protons speed up. The magnetic flux density is 1.4 T. Show that the frequency of the alternating potential difference must be about 20 MHz. The protons leave the cyclotron when the radius of their path is 0.36 m. Calculate the kinetic energy of the protons as they leave, in MeV. The peak potential difference between the dees is 40 kV. Calculate the minimum number of times a proton must cross the gap to reach this kinetic energy.
items.ms: IC1 An electric field in the gap between the dees accelerates the protons (increases their kinetic energy) each time they cross the gap IC2 There is no electric field inside the dees, so the protons move at constant speed there IC3 The magnetic field exerts a force on the protons perpendicular to their velocity, which provides the centripetal force, so they move in a semicircle inside each dee IC4 The p.d. reverses while the protons are inside a dee, so the field in the gap is in the accelerating direction every time they cross it IC5 As the speed increases the radius increases (r = p/BQ), so the protons spiral outwards IC6 The time for each semicircle (πm/BQ) does not depend on the speed or radius, so the p.d. can have a constant frequency Use of r = p/BQ (or BQv = mv²/r) with v = 2πr/T (or v = rω) The frequency of the p.d. equals the frequency of revolution: f = 1/T = BQ/2πm f = 2.13 × 10⁷ Hz Use of r = p/BQ (p = 8.06 × 10⁻²⁰ N s) Use of Ek = p²/2m (or v = p/m and Ek = ½mv²) Conversion from J to MeV, Ek = 12 MeV Maximum energy gained per crossing = 40 keV (6.4 × 10⁻¹⁵ J) Number of crossings = 305
items.why: S114 is asked in every session but one; cyclotron 6-mark answers appeared in Jan2021 and Jan2025, the Jan2021 report said candidates missed why the frequency is constant, and Jan2025 Q17(b) and Jan2020 Q19(b) calculated the timing and number of passes.

items.question: Electrons are accelerated from rest through a potential difference V. They then move at right angles to a uniform magnetic field of flux density B, in a circle of radius r. The accelerating potential difference is increased to 4V and the magnetic flux density is reduced to B/2. What is the new radius? r 2r 4r 8r
items.ms: eV = p²/2m, so p ∝ √V, and r = p/BQ ∝ √V/B. New radius = √4 ÷ ½ × r = 4r. A multiplies by the change in B instead of dividing. B ignores the change in B. D leaves out the square root (r ∝ V/B).
items.why: The chain V → Ek → p → r = p/BQ is one of the digest's standard calculation chains; Jun2026 Q10 changed speed and B together, so combined changes are likely again.

items.question: In a proton-therapy machine, an electromagnet bends a beam of protons through a circular arc. A particle of mass m and charge Q moves with speed v at right angles to a uniform magnetic field of flux density B. Derive the equation r = p/BQ for the radius r of the particle's path, where p is the momentum of the particle.

items.question: In radiocarbon dating by accelerator mass spectrometry, carbon ions, each with charge +3e, leave an accelerator with a kinetic energy of 7.2 MeV. They enter a uniform magnetic field at right angles to the field and follow semicircular paths, as shown, so that ions of the isotopes carbon-12 (¹²C), carbon-13 (¹³C) and carbon-14 (¹⁴C) reach separate detectors. mass of a carbon-14 ion = 14u mass of a carbon-13 ion = 13u u = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg Show that the momentum of a carbon-14 ion is about 2.3 × 10⁻¹⁹ N s. The carbon-14 ions follow a path of radius 0.85 m. Calculate the magnetic flux density. The carbon-13 ions enter the field with the same kinetic energy and the same charge. Explain why their path has a smaller radius. Calculate the distance between the points where the carbon-13 ions and the carbon-14 ions reach the detectors.
items.ms: Conversion of 7.2 MeV to J (1.15 × 10⁻¹² J) Use of Ek = p²/2m p = 2.31 × 10⁻¹⁹ N s Use of r = p/BQ with Q = 3e (4.8 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) B = 0.57 T A carbon-13 ion has a smaller mass, so it has a smaller momentum for the same kinetic energy (p = √(2mEk)) r = p/BQ, and B and Q are the same, so the radius is smaller r ∝ √m for the same Ek and Q, so r(carbon-13) = 0.85 m × √(13/14) = 0.819 m Distance between detectors = difference in diameters = 2(r₁₄ − r₁₃) Distance = 0.062 m
items.why: Using r = p/BQ came up in Jun2023 Q12(b), Oct2024 Q18(a) and Jun2026 Q14(b) (identifying an ion from m/Q); separating two isotopes with the same charge and energy is a new context that also needs r ∝ √m.

items.question: The diagram shows the track of an electron in a gas-filled detector. There is a uniform magnetic field of flux density 3.0 mT perpendicular to the page. The track is a spiral made of semicircles. Points A, B and C lie on the track, on a straight line through the centres of the semicircles. The scale bar shows 2.0 cm. Explain why the radius of the track decreases. Deduce whether the magnetic field is directed into or out of the page. By taking measurements from the diagram, determine the momentum of the electron as it travels from A to B. Calculate the kinetic energy of the electron as it travels from A to B. Give your answer in eV. Determine the percentage of its kinetic energy that the electron loses between the semicircle AB and the semicircle BC.
items.ms: The electron loses (kinetic) energy as it ionises the gas atoms so its momentum decreases; r = p/BQ with B and Q constant, so r decreases The electron travels from A towards C (and the centre), because the radius must decrease along its path Fleming's left-hand rule applied with the current opposite to the electron's velocity, and the force towards the centre of the semicircle The field is out of the page Measures AB and the scale bar, and applies the scale: AB = 9.0 cm r = AB/2 = 4.5 cm (0.045 m) Use of r = p/BQ p = 2.2 × 10⁻²³ N s Use of Ek = p²/2m (or v = p/m and Ek = ½mv²) Ek = 1.6 × 10³ eV Ek ∝ p² ∝ r², so Ek(BC)/Ek(AB) = (BC/AB)² (= 0.71) Percentage lost = 29%
items.why: r = p/BQ came up in 15 of 19 sessions; measuring a radius from a track (Jun2022 Q14(a)) and a spiral of decreasing radius (Oct2021 Q18(b)) both recur, but the energy lost per turn has not been asked.

path: Unit 4 Further Mechanics, Fields and Particles
Nuclear and Particle Physics

items.question: The diagram shows tracks in a bubble chamber. There is a uniform magnetic field directed into the page. A charged particle enters from the left and its track ends at X. Two tracks start at Y. Which conclusion can be made from the diagram? The particle that entered from the left had no charge. The two particles produced at Y have charges of the same sign. Momentum was not conserved in the interaction at X. A neutral particle travelled from X to Y.
items.ms: Only charged particles ionise the liquid and leave tracks, so a particle with no charge must have carried the momentum from X to Y, where it decayed. A: the entering particle left a track, so it was charged. B: the tracks from Y curve in opposite directions in the same field, so the charges have opposite signs. C: momentum is always conserved; the neutral particle carries it.
items.why: Interpreting tracks with a missing neutral particle recurs (Jan2024 Q12, Jun2025 Q14(c), Oct2025 Q3); S116 has come up in 13 of 19 sessions.

items.name: Conservation laws in particle interactions; interpreting tracks
path: Unit 4 Further Mechanics, Fields and Particles
Nuclear and Particle Physics
S116 - apply conservation of charge, energy and mome
items.question: A lambda particle (Λ⁰) at rest decays into a proton and a negative pion: Λ⁰ → p + π⁻. Which statement about the proton and the pion must be correct? They have kinetic energies of equal size. They have equal speeds. They move in opposite directions with momenta of equal size. Their total kinetic energy is equal to the rest energy of the Λ⁰.
items.ms: The Λ⁰ has zero momentum, so the two products must have equal and opposite momenta. A and B: the proton and the pion have different masses, so equal momenta give different speeds and different kinetic energies. D: most of the rest energy of the Λ⁰ becomes the rest energy of the proton and the pion; only the difference becomes kinetic energy.
items.why: Applying conservation of momentum to a decay came up in Oct2025 Q3 and Oct2025 Q18(b); D tests the energy bookkeeping that Jan2022 Q16(c) needed.

items.name: Conservation laws in particle interactions; interpreting tracks
path: Unit 4 Further Mechanics, Fields and Particles
Nuclear and Particle Physics

items.question: The diagram shows the tracks produced when a neutral kaon (K⁰) decays at D into two pions, π⁺ and π⁻. The K⁰ was produced at O. The dashed line shows the path of the K⁰. There is a uniform magnetic field directed into the page. The tracks make angles of 25° and 40° with the path of the K⁰. Explain why there is no track between O and D. The momentum of the particle making track 1 is 2.50 × 10⁻¹⁹ N s. Calculate the momentum of the particle making track 2. Calculate the momentum of the K⁰. Deduce which track is made by the π⁺.
items.ms: The K⁰ is neutral (uncharged), so it does not ionise the liquid Components perpendicular to the K⁰ path are equal and opposite: p₁ sin 25° = p₂ sin 40° p₂ = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ N s p(K⁰) = p₁ cos 25° + p₂ cos 40° p = 3.5 × 10⁻¹⁹ N s Fleming's left-hand rule: for a positive particle in this field, the force is to the left of its velocity / it curves anticlockwise Track 1
items.why: Momentum conservation at a decay vertex came up in Oct2021 Q18(e) (vector triangle) and Jan2022 Q16(c); a numerical two-dimensional resolution at a neutral-particle decay has not been asked.

items.name: Conservation laws in particle interactions; interpreting tracks
path: Unit 4 Further Mechanics, Fields and Particles
Nuclear and Particle Physics
S116 - apply conservation of charge, energy and mome
items.question: The diagram shows tracks in a bubble chamber. There is a uniform magnetic field directed into the page. A positive pion (π⁺) enters at the bottom left, slows down and comes to rest at A, where it decays. The track from A to B is made by an antimuon (μ⁺), which comes to rest at B and decays. The track starting at B is made by a positron (e⁺). Explain how the tracks show that the antimuon and the positron have charges of the same sign. Only one track leaves A. Explain why another particle must also be produced at A, and deduce its charge. In many bubble-chamber photographs like this one, every antimuon track from A to B has the same length. The positron tracks starting at B have a range of different lengths and initial radii. Explain what this suggests about the number of particles produced at A and at B. The rest mass of the π⁺ is 139.6 MeV/c² and the rest mass of the μ⁺ is 105.7 MeV/c². The other particle produced at A has negligible mass. The antimuon has a kinetic energy of 4.1 MeV. Calculate the energy of the other particle produced at A.
items.ms: Both tracks curve in the same direction (anticlockwise) / have the same sense of rotation In the same magnetic field, the force on each is in the same direction relative to its velocity, so the charges have the same sign (Fleming's left-hand rule) The pion is at rest at A, so the total momentum before the decay is zero The antimuon moves away with momentum, so another particle must move in the opposite direction with momentum of equal size (conservation of momentum) It leaves no track, so it is neutral; charge is conserved: +1 = +1 + 0 At A, two particles are produced from zero momentum, so they have equal and opposite momenta; with conservation of energy, this fixes the energy of each So every antimuon has the same kinetic energy, and the same track length At B, the positron's kinetic energy varies, so the energy (and momentum) is shared between more than two particles So at least two neutral particles (with no tracks) are also produced at B (neutrinos) Energy released = (139.6 − 105.7) MeV = 33.9 MeV Energy of the other particle = 33.9 − 4.1 = 29.8 MeV
items.why: S116 has come up in 13 of 19 sessions; deducing an unseen neutral particle from momentum (Jun2025 Q14(c), Oct2025 Q18(b)) recurs, but the fixed antimuon energy against the spread of positron energies, the classic evidence for extra neutrinos, has never been asked.

items.name: Why high energies are needed to investigate nucleon structure
path: Unit 4 Further Mechanics, Fields and Particles
Nuclear and Particle Physics
S117 - why high energies are required to investigate
items.question: High-energy electrons are fired at protons and neutrons to investigate their structure. Why must the electrons have a very high energy? so that their de Broglie wavelength is similar to or smaller than the size of a nucleon so that they can overcome the electrostatic repulsion of the nucleus so that they have enough energy to create new particles in the collisions so that their de Broglie wavelength is much larger than a nucleon and they diffract around it
items.ms: A high energy gives a large momentum and so a short de Broglie wavelength (λ = h/p), which is needed to resolve detail about 10⁻¹⁵ m across. B: electrons are attracted, not repelled, by nuclei. C is a reason for high energies in collisions, but not for investigating structure. D: a wavelength much larger than a nucleon could not resolve its structure.
items.why: This reason was asked as an MCQ in Jun2021, Jan2024, Jun2025 and twice in Jan2026; Jun2023 used 'to create new particles' as the distractor.

items.name: Why high energies are needed to investigate nucleon structure
path: Unit 4 Further Mechanics, Fields and Particles
Nuclear and Particle Physics
S117 - why high energies are required to investigate
items.question: To investigate the structure inside a proton, the de Broglie wavelength of the electrons used must be less than the diameter of the proton, 1.7 × 10⁻¹⁵ m. For electrons of these energies, E = pc. Which is the lowest of these electron energies that would be suitable? 1 MeV 10 MeV 100 MeV 1 GeV
items.ms: λ = h/p = hc/E, so E must be more than hc/λ = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3.00 × 10⁸) ÷ 1.7 × 10⁻¹⁵ = 1.2 × 10⁻¹⁰ J = 731 MeV. Only 1 GeV is above this (λ = 1.2 × 10⁻¹⁵ m). 100 MeV gives λ = 1.2 × 10⁻¹⁴ m, about seven times the diameter; 1 MeV and 10 MeV give even longer wavelengths.
items.why: S117 has come up in 10 of 19 sessions, always qualitatively; putting a number on 'high energy' links it to λ = h/p, the link the reports say candidates fail to make.

items.name: Why high energies are needed to investigate nucleon structure
path: Unit 4 Further Mechanics, Fields and Particles
Nuclear and Particle Physics
S117 - why high energies are required to investigate
items.question: Electron-scattering experiments have been used to investigate the structure of the proton. For electrons of these energies, E = pc, where p is the momentum of the electron. The diameter of a proton is about 1.7 × 10⁻¹⁵ m. In 1968, electrons of energy 20 GeV were scattered from protons at the Stanford Linear Accelerator Center. Show that the de Broglie wavelength of these electrons was about 6 × 10⁻¹⁷ m. In the 1950s, electrons of energy 0.50 GeV were used. These experiments measured the size of the proton but did not show any structure inside it. Explain why the 20 GeV electrons could show structure inside the proton but the 0.50 GeV electrons could not. Modern experiments collide beams of particles travelling in opposite directions, instead of firing particles at a stationary target. Explain an advantage of colliding beams.
items.ms: Conversion of 20 GeV to J (3.2 × 10⁻⁹ J) Use of p = E/c and λ = h/p λ = 6.22 × 10⁻¹⁷ m λ for 0.50 GeV electrons = 2.5 × 10⁻¹⁵ m (40 times larger) This is about the same as the diameter of the proton, so the electrons are diffracted (scattered) by the proton as a whole, which gives its size To resolve detail inside the proton, the wavelength must be much smaller than the proton 6.2 × 10⁻¹⁷ m is much smaller than 1.7 × 10⁻¹⁵ m, so the 20 GeV electrons can resolve structure (quarks) inside the proton The total momentum before the collision is small (zero if the momenta are equal and opposite) So the products need little momentum or kinetic energy, and more (almost all) of the energy is available to create new particles
items.why: S117 has come up in 10 of 19 sessions, mostly as MCQs, with 3-mark explanations in Jan2020 Q19(c) and Jun2024 Q16(c); comparing two electron energies tests the wavelength–resolution link, and colliding beams recur (Jun2022, Oct2022, Jan2023).

items.question: The weber (Wb) is the unit of magnetic flux. Which of the following is equivalent to the weber? kg A⁻¹ s⁻² kg m A⁻¹ s⁻² kg m² A⁻¹ s⁻³ kg m² A⁻¹ s⁻²
items.ms: φ = BA, so Wb = T m² = N A⁻¹ m⁻¹ × m² = N m A⁻¹ = kg m² s⁻² A⁻¹ (also Wb = V s). A is the tesla in base units; B is T m (N A⁻¹); C is the volt.
items.why: Units come up as MCQs on this topic (the tesla in base units Oct2022, a unit of flux Oct2023, the tesla in N, A and m Oct2025); the weber in base units has not been asked.

path: Unit 4 Further Mechanics, Fields and Particles
Electric and Magnetic Fields

items.question: A flat square coil of 120 turns and side 5.0 cm is in a uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.30 T. At first the plane of the coil is perpendicular to the field. The coil is then rotated through 60° about an axis in the plane of the coil and perpendicular to the field. What is the magnitude of the change in the magnetic flux linkage of the coil? 0.012 Wb 0.045 Wb 0.078 Wb 0.090 Wb
items.ms: At first Nφ = 120 × 0.30 × (0.050 m)² = 0.090 Wb. After the rotation the normal to the coil is at 60° to the field, so Nφ = 0.090 × cos 60° = 0.045 Wb and the change is 0.045 Wb. A uses sin 60° for the final flux linkage (0.078 Wb) and subtracts; C is that sin 60° value itself; D is the initial flux linkage (the change for a 90° rotation).
items.why: Flux linkage after a rotation was an MCQ in Oct2021 (through π); a part rotation needing the component of B along the normal (the digest's 'field through a tilted coil', Oct2025 Q14) has not been an MCQ.

items.question: An MRI scanner produces a uniform magnetic field of flux density 1.5 T. A technician checks the field with a flat circular coil of 40 turns and diameter 2.4 cm. The plane of the coil is perpendicular to the field. Calculate the magnetic flux linkage of the coil.

items.name: F = Bqv sin θ; Fleming's left-hand rule on charged particles

items.question: An alpha particle moves at 3.5 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ at an angle of 35° to a uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.60 T. What is the magnitude of the magnetic force on the alpha particle? 1.9 × 10⁻¹³ N 2.8 × 10⁻¹³ N 3.9 × 10⁻¹³ N 5.5 × 10⁻¹³ N
items.ms: F = Bqv sin θ = 0.60 × (2 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹) × 3.5 × 10⁶ × sin 35° = 3.9 × 10⁻¹³ N. A uses a charge of e; B uses e and cos 35°; D uses cos 35°.
items.why: F = Bqv has come up in 12 of 19 sessions; Oct2024 set an angle between v and B, and the alpha particle's charge of 2e (Jan2026 Q11) is a known trap.

items.name: F = Bqv sin θ; Fleming's left-hand rule on charged particles
path: Unit 4 Further Mechanics, Fields and Particles

items.question: A beam of electrons travels horizontally towards the east. A uniform magnetic field deflects the beam vertically upwards. What is the direction of the magnetic field? towards the south towards the north vertically downwards vertically upwards
items.ms: Electrons are negative, so the conventional current is towards the west. Fleming's left-hand rule with the current west and the force upwards gives a field towards the south. B treats the electrons as positive (current east). C and D would deflect the beam horizontally (to the south and to the north).
items.why: Direction by Fleming's left-hand rule is asked most sessions (Jun2026 Q14(a), Jan2026 Q18(b), Jun2025 Q11(b)); reversing the current for a negative charge is the commonest slip.

path: Unit 4 Further Mechanics, Fields and Particles
Electric and Magnetic Fields
S106 - use the equation F  Bqv sin and apply Fleming
items.question: Cosmic rays include high-energy protons that arrive at the Earth from space. Above the equator, the Earth's magnetic field is horizontal and directed towards the north, with a flux density of 3.2 × 10⁻⁵ T. A proton travels vertically downwards towards the equator at a speed of 2.4 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹. Calculate the magnitude of the magnetic force on the proton. State the direction of the magnetic force on the proton. Near the magnetic poles the Earth's magnetic field is almost vertical. Explain why protons travelling vertically downwards near the poles are deflected much less than protons travelling vertically downwards above the equator. State why the magnetic force does not change the speed of the proton.
items.ms: Use of F = Bqv F = 1.2 × 10⁻¹⁶ N Towards the east Near the poles the velocity of the proton is (almost) parallel to the field, so θ ≈ 0 F = Bqv sin θ, so the force (and the deflection) is (almost) zero The force is always at right angles to the velocity (so no work is done on the proton)
items.why: F = Bqv calculations recur (Jan2026 Q11, Jun2025 Q11(a)); the sin θ factor for motion along the field and the fact that the magnetic force does no work have not been examined directly.

items.name: F = Bqv sin θ; Fleming's left-hand rule on charged particles
path: Unit 4 Further Mechanics, Fields and Particles
Electric and Magnetic Fields
S106 - use the equation F  Bqv sin and apply Fleming
items.question: An electromagnetic flow meter measures the speed of blood in an artery without entering the blood vessel. The artery is placed in a uniform magnetic field, at right angles to the field. Two electrodes, X and Y, touch the outside of the artery wall on opposite sides of the artery, as shown. Blood contains positive and negative ions, which move with the blood. Explain why X becomes positive with respect to Y when blood flows through the artery. Explain why the potential difference (p.d.) between X and Y rises to a constant value. Show that the speed v of the blood is given by v = V/(Bd) where V is the p.d. between X and Y, B is the magnetic flux density and d is the diameter of the artery. The magnetic flux density is 0.080 T, the diameter of the artery is 4.0 mm and the p.d. between X and Y is 0.11 mV. Calculate the speed of the blood. A technician says that, for the same speed of flow, the meter will give a larger p.d. for blood with a greater concentration of ions. Comment on this statement.
items.ms: The ions are charges moving at right angles to the magnetic field, so there is a (magnetic) force on them By Fleming's left-hand rule the force on positive ions is towards X (upwards in the diagram) and the force on negative ions is towards Y The separated charges produce an electric field across the artery The electric force on each ion is opposite to the magnetic force The electric field (and force) increases as more charge is separated When the electric force equals the magnetic force, there is no further deflection of ions, so the p.d. stops rising Magnetic force = electric force: BQv = EQ Use of E = V/d to give v = V/(Bd) Use of v = V/(Bd) with V in volts and d in metres v = 0.34 m s⁻¹ Both the magnetic force and the electric force on an ion are proportional to its charge, so the charge cancels (v = V/(Bd) does not depend on the charge or the number of ions) So the final p.d. depends only on v, B and d, and the technician is wrong More ions would only make the p.d. reach its final value sooner
items.why: Balancing electric and magnetic forces on moving charges (velocity selector Oct2022 Q18(b), Thomson Jan2023 Q17, e/m Oct2023 Q22) recurs; a blood flow meter puts the same physics in an unseen medical context.

items.name: F = BIl sin θ; Fleming's left-hand rule on conductors
path: Unit 4 Further Mechanics, Fields and Particles

items.question: A straight wire of length 6.0 cm carries a current of 3.2 A. The wire is at an angle of 30° to a uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.25 T. What is the magnitude of the force on the wire? 0.024 N 0.042 N 0.048 N 2.4 N
items.ms: F = BIl sin θ = 0.25 × 3.2 × 0.060 × sin 30° = 0.024 N. B uses cos 30°; C ignores the angle; D uses the length in cm.
items.why: F = BIl sin θ at an angle was an MCQ in Jun2022 and Jan2026; mixing up sin and cos is the main examiner-report pitfall (Jan2025).

items.name: F = BIl sin θ; Fleming's left-hand rule on conductors
path: Unit 4 Further Mechanics, Fields and Particles
Electric and Magnetic Fields
S107 - use the equation F  BIl sin and apply Fleming
items.question: A horizontal wire passes between the poles of a magnet that rests on a top-pan balance. The wire is at right angles to the magnetic field. When the current in the wire is 2.5 A, the balance reading increases by 1.24 g. The current is reversed and increased to 5.0 A. How does the balance reading now compare with the reading when there is no current? It is greater by 1.24 g. It is greater by 2.48 g. It is less by 1.24 g. It is less by 2.48 g.
items.ms: F = BIl, so doubling the current doubles the force on the wire and, by Newton's third law, the force on the magnet. Reversing the current reverses both forces, so the reading is less by 2 × 1.24 = 2.48 g. A and B ignore the reversal; C ignores the doubling.
items.why: The top-pan balance set-up was asked in Oct2023 Q13 and Jun2025 Q13; reversing the current with Newton's third law makes it a quick conceptual check.

items.name: F = BIl sin θ; Fleming's left-hand rule on conductors
path: Unit 4 Further Mechanics, Fields and Particles
Electric and Magnetic Fields
S107 - use the equation F  BIl sin and apply Fleming
items.question: A rectangular coil of 80 turns measures 4.0 cm × 2.5 cm and carries a current of 0.15 A. The plane of the coil is parallel to a uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.20 T, with the 4.0 cm sides at right angles to the field. The coil can turn about an axis through its centre, parallel to the 4.0 cm sides. What is the resultant moment on the coil about this axis? 3.0 × 10⁻⁵ N m 1.2 × 10⁻³ N m 2.4 × 10⁻³ N m 4.8 × 10⁻³ N m
items.ms: Force on each 4.0 cm side = NBIl = 80 × 0.20 × 0.15 × 0.040 = 0.096 N, in opposite directions. Each acts 1.25 cm from the axis, so the moment = 2 × 0.096 × 0.0125 = 2.4 × 10⁻³ N m. The 2.5 cm sides are parallel to the field, so there is no force on them. A leaves out N; B includes only one side; D takes each force as acting 2.5 cm from the axis.
items.why: Oct2024 Q15(a) asked for the resultant moment on a motor coil, and the examiners' report noted that only half of those who found the force dealt with both sides; an MCQ version with N turns is likely.

items.question: The diagram shows a view from above of a simple electromagnetic launcher. A light aluminium rod JK rests across two horizontal metal rails 5.0 cm apart. The rails and rod are in a uniform vertical magnetic field of flux density 0.30 T. A capacitor of capacitance 0.010 F is charged to 50 V. When the switch is closed, the capacitor discharges through the rails and the rod. Explain the direction in which the rod moves. Show that the impulse given to the rod is BlQ, where B is the magnetic flux density, l is the distance between the rails and Q is the charge that flows through the rod. Calculate the charge stored on the capacitor before the switch is closed. The mass of the rod is 2.5 g. All of the charge flows through the rod while it is on the rails, and resistive forces are negligible. Calculate the speed of the rod as it leaves the rails. Compare the kinetic energy of the rod with the energy that was stored in the capacitor. Comment on your answer.
items.ms: The current in the rod is from J to K, at right angles to the field By Fleming's left-hand rule the force on the rod is to the right (away from the capacitor) Force on the rod F = BIl Impulse = ΣFΔt = Bl ΣIΔt, and ΣIΔt = Q, so impulse = BlQ Q = CV = 0.50 C Use of impulse = BlQ Use of impulse = change in momentum = mv v = 3.0 m s⁻¹ Energy stored = ½CV² = 12.5 J and kinetic energy = ½mv² = 0.011 J Only about 0.09% of the energy becomes kinetic energy; most is dissipated as thermal energy by the current in the resistance of the rod and rails
items.why: A rod on rails was asked in Oct2025 Q22; driving it from a capacitor links F = BIl to impulse and capacitor energy, the kind of synoptic Section B question Unit 4 favours.

items.question: A student uses the apparatus shown to measure the magnetic flux density between the poles of a magnet. The magnet rests on a top-pan balance. A stiff horizontal wire is clamped so that it passes between the poles, at right angles to the magnetic field. The wire does not touch the magnet. When there is a current in the wire, the balance reading increases. Deduce the direction of the current in the wire. Explain your answer. The length of wire between the poles is 5.0 cm. The student measures the increase Δm in the balance reading for different currents I. The results are shown in the table. Plot a graph of Δm against I on the grid. Use your graph to determine the magnetic flux density between the poles. The poles of the magnet are 5.0 cm long, so the student used l = 5.0 cm. In fact the magnetic field also extends a short distance beyond the edges of the poles. Explain how this affects the value of the magnetic flux density determined by the student. The student turns the wire in the horizontal plane so that it makes an angle of 60° with the magnetic field. Assume that the length of wire in the field does not change. items.question: A bar magnet hangs from a spring so that its lower end is just above a vertical coil. The coil is connected to a data logger, which records the e.m.f. across the coil. The magnet is pulled down a short distance and released. It oscillates vertically, and its lower end moves into and out of the top of the coil. The graph shows how the e.m.f. ε across the coil varies with time t after the magnet is released. Explain the shape of the graph. State one change to the apparatus that would increase the maximum e.m.f. recorded.
items.ms: IC1 As the magnet moves, the magnetic flux linkage with the coil changes (or the wires of the coil cut magnetic field lines) IC2 An e.m.f. is induced that is proportional to the rate of change of flux linkage (Faraday's law) IC3 The e.m.f. is zero when the magnet is momentarily at rest at the top and bottom of its oscillation, because the flux linkage is not changing IC4 The e.m.f. is greatest when the magnet passes through its equilibrium position, where its speed is greatest IC5 The e.m.f. changes direction each half oscillation, because the magnet changes direction, so the flux linkage increases and then decreases IC6 The peak e.m.f. decreases because the amplitude (and maximum speed) of the oscillation decreases as energy is dissipated; the e.m.f. has the same period as the oscillation Any one of: a coil with more turns; a stronger magnet; a stiffer spring (so the magnet moves faster for the same amplitude)

items.question: Coil P is connected to an alternating supply. Coil Q is placed next to P, on the same axis, and connected to an oscilloscope. Which change would not increase the amplitude of the e.m.f. induced in Q? Reverse the connections between P and the supply. Increase the frequency of the supply. Place an iron rod through both coils. Use a coil Q with more turns.
items.ms: Reversing the connections only reverses the direction of the alternating current at each instant; its amplitude and rate of change are unchanged, so the amplitude of the e.m.f. is unchanged. B increases the rate of change of current and so of flux linkage; C increases the flux linking Q; D increases N in ε = N dφ/dt.

items.question: Two coils are wound on the same iron core. The graph shows how the current I in the first coil varies with time t. Which graph shows how the e.m.f. ε induced in the second coil varies with time? Graph A Graph B Graph C Graph D
items.ms: The induced e.m.f. is proportional to the rate of change of current. The current rises at a steady rate for 3 ms and then falls three times as fast for 1 ms, so the e.m.f. is constant for 3 ms and then three times as large, in the opposite direction, for 1 ms. items.question: Two coils, P and Q, are wound on an iron core, as shown. Coil P is connected to a battery and a switch. Coil Q is connected to a sensitive centre-zero ammeter. When the switch is closed, the ammeter needle deflects briefly and then returns to zero, although there is still a current in coil P. Explain these observations. Describe what the ammeter shows when the switch is opened again.
