items.question: Some theatres have a hearing loop for people who use hearing aids. A loop of wire runs around the edge of the floor. An amplifier sends an alternating current, which carries the sound signal, through the loop. A hearing aid contains a small coil called a telecoil. The e.m.f. induced in the telecoil is amplified and turned back into sound. Explain how an alternating e.m.f. is induced in the telecoil. When a steady note is played, the magnetic flux density B at the telecoil varies with time t as shown in the graph. The telecoil has 4000 turns and a cross-sectional area of 3.0 × 10⁻⁵ m². Its axis is parallel to the magnetic field. Use the graph to determine the maximum e.m.f. induced in the telecoil. A hearing-aid user finds that the sound from the telecoil almost disappears when she lies down, so that the axis of the telecoil is horizontal. At her position the magnetic field of the loop is vertical. Suggest why the sound almost disappears.
items.ms: The current in the loop produces a magnetic field that passes through the telecoil The current is alternating, so the magnetic field changes (in size and direction) So the magnetic flux linkage with the telecoil changes An e.m.f. is induced (Faraday's law), proportional to the rate of change of flux linkage The e.m.f. alternates at the same frequency as the current in the loop Tangent drawn where B = 0 (steepest part) and its gradient determined (about 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ T s⁻¹) Use of ε = NA dB/dt ε = 6.0 × 10⁻⁵ V The field is now parallel to the plane of the telecoil, so (almost) no magnetic flux passes through it and the flux linkage is (almost) zero So the flux linkage hardly changes and (almost) no e.m.f. is induced

items.question: A coil of 400 turns has a cross-sectional area of 3.0 cm². It is in a uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.25 T, parallel to the axis of the coil. The field decreases steadily to zero in 50 ms. What is the magnitude of the e.m.f. induced in the coil? 1.5 × 10⁻³ V 0.60 V 6.0 V 60 V
items.ms: ε = NΔφ/Δt = 400 × 0.25 × 3.0 × 10⁻⁴ / 0.050 = 0.60 V. A leaves out N; C uses 5.0 ms; D converts 3.0 cm² to 3.0 × 10⁻² m².

items.question: An aluminium ring rests on top of a solenoid, around the end of the solenoid's iron core. The solenoid is connected to a d.c. supply and a switch. When the switch is closed, the ring jumps upwards. Which change would stop the ring jumping when the switch is closed? Increase the current in the solenoid. Reverse the connections to the d.c. supply. Turn the ring upside down. Cut a narrow gap in the ring.
items.ms: With a gap there is still an e.m.f. but no complete circuit, so there is no induced current and no force on the ring. A increases the rate of change of flux, so the ring jumps higher. B reverses both the field and the induced current, so by Lenz's law the ring is still repelled. C changes neither the flux linkage nor the current.
items.why: Lenz's law is asked in most sessions (Jun2026 Q13(a), Jan2026 Q17(c)); the jumping ring checks that a reversed supply still repels and that a complete circuit is needed for a current.

items.question: A square coil of 25 turns and side 6.0 cm is pulled at a constant speed of 0.50 m s⁻¹ out of a region of uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.36 T. The plane of the coil is perpendicular to the field, and the coil moves parallel to two of its sides. What is the e.m.f. induced in the coil while it is leaving the field? 0.011 V 0.032 V 0.27 V 0.54 V
items.ms: Only the side still in the field cuts field lines: ε = NBlv = 25 × 0.36 × 0.060 × 0.50 = 0.27 V (or ε = NBA/t with t = 0.060/0.50 = 0.12 s). A leaves out N; B is the flux linkage NBA (in Wb), not an e.m.f.; D adds e.m.f.s for two sides, but only one side is in the field.
items.why: Motional e.m.f. was asked in Oct2023 Q17, Jan2024 Q16 and Oct2025 Q14; a coil of N turns leaving a field has not been an MCQ.

items.question: A student uses a flat circular search coil to measure the magnetic flux density of the Earth's magnetic field. The coil has 600 turns and a diameter of 10.0 cm, and it is connected to a data logger. The coil is placed with its axis along the direction of the Earth's magnetic field. It is then quickly turned through 180° about a diameter. The graph shows how the e.m.f. ε across the coil varies with time t. Explain why an e.m.f. is induced in the coil while it is being turned. Explain why the area under the graph is equal to the change in flux linkage of the coil. Use the graph to determine the magnetic flux density of the Earth's magnetic field. The student repeats the experiment, turning the coil through 180° in a shorter time. State how the graph changes.
items.ms: The angle between the field and the coil changes, so the flux linkage changes (from NBA to −NBA) An e.m.f. is induced proportional to the rate of change of flux linkage (Faraday's law) ε = Δ(Nφ)/Δt (in magnitude), so in a short time Δt the change in flux linkage is εΔt εΔt is the area of a thin strip under the graph, so the total area is the total change in flux linkage Area under the graph determined, e.g. by counting squares (about 4.6 × 10⁻⁴ V s) Change in flux linkage = 2NBA (the flux linkage reverses) A = π × (0.050 m)² = 7.85 × 10⁻³ m² B = 4.9 × 10⁻⁵ T The pulse is taller and narrower, with the same area
items.why: S110 is asked in 18 of 19 sessions; using the area under an e.m.f.–time graph as the change in flux linkage (a flip-coil measurement of the Earth's field) has never been asked.

items.question: A model generator has a rectangular coil that is turned at a constant rate between the poles of a magnet. The coil has 250 turns and measures 4.0 cm × 3.0 cm. The coil is connected to an oscilloscope, and the trace shows how the e.m.f. across the coil varies with time. The oscilloscope settings are: Y-gain 2.0 V div⁻¹ time base 10 ms div⁻¹ Explain why the e.m.f. is zero at the instant when the plane of the coil is at right angles to the magnetic field. Use the trace to answer the following. Determine the peak e.m.f. Show that the angular velocity of the coil is about 160 rad s⁻¹. Show that the magnetic flux density between the poles is about 0.1 T. A lamp is connected across the coil. The motor that turns the coil now has to do more work to keep the coil turning at the same rate. Explain why. The lamp is disconnected and the rate of rotation of the coil is halved. Sketch, on the screen shown, the trace that would now be seen.
items.ms: The flux linkage is a maximum at this instant Its rate of change is zero (the sides of the coil move parallel to the field and do not cut field lines), so ε = −d(Nφ)/dt = 0 Peak e.m.f. = 2.6 div × 2.0 V div⁻¹ = 5.2 V Period = 4.0 div × 10 ms div⁻¹ = 40 ms ω = 2π/T = 157 rad s⁻¹ A = 1.2 × 10⁻³ m² Use of peak e.m.f. = BANω B = 0.11 T There is now a current in the coil, and there is a force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field By Lenz's law these forces oppose the rotation of the coil (the change producing the current) The work done against these forces is transferred to the lamp as electrical energy Peak halved: amplitude 1.3 div Period doubled: 8.0 div, sinusoidal shape
items.why: The rotating-coil generator has come up in each of the last three sessions (Oct2025 Q14, Jan2026 Q17, Jun2026 Q20); reading the peak and period from an oscilloscope trace and working back to B is an untested direction.

items.question: On a drop-tower ride, a car carrying passengers falls freely and then passes through a braking section. In the braking section, copper fins fixed to the car pass through narrow gaps between two rows of strong permanent magnets fixed to the tower. The magnetic field in each gap is horizontal and at right angles to the fins. Explain how the magnets produce a braking force on the car. The car enters the braking section at a speed of 28.0 m s⁻¹. The magnetic flux density in the gap is 0.85 T. The part of a fin in the field has a horizontal length of 0.20 m, at right angles to both the field and the direction of motion. Calculate the e.m.f. induced across this length of the fin. The mass of the car and passengers is 1500 kg. In the braking section the speed of the car decreases from 28.0 m s⁻¹ to 8.0 m s⁻¹ in 3.2 s. Calculate the average braking force on the car. Explain why the magnetic brakes alone cannot bring the car to rest. The designers want a larger braking force at the same speed. Suggest two changes they could make to the fins or the magnets.
items.ms: IC1 As a fin moves through a gap, it cuts magnetic field lines (the flux linkage with parts of the fin changes) IC2 An e.m.f. is induced in the fin (Faraday's law) IC3 The fin is a conductor, so (eddy) currents circulate in the fin IC4 There is a force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field (F = BIl) IC5 By Lenz's law the induced current opposes the change producing it, so the force on the fins (and the car) is upwards, opposing the motion IC6 The kinetic energy of the car is transferred to thermal energy in the fins (by the currents in their resistance) Use of ε = Blv (or ε = Δφ/Δt with the area swept per second = lv) ε = 4.8 V Use of impulse = change in momentum, e.g. Δp = 1500 × (28.0 − 8.0) Resultant force = Δp/Δt, and braking force = resultant force + weight Braking force = 2.4 × 10⁴ N The induced e.m.f. (and current) is proportional to the speed of the fins (the rate of change of flux linkage) So the braking force decreases as the car slows down When the braking force has fallen to the size of the weight, the resultant force is zero and the car continues at a constant (terminal) speed At zero speed there would be no braking force at all Stronger magnets (larger B) Thicker fins, or fins of a metal with lower resistivity (larger currents) Larger fins or more magnets (more of each fin in the field)
items.why: Eddy-current braking appears in 7 of 19 papers (e.g. Oct2021 Q15, Jan2022 Q18, Jun2022 Q18) and induction is the commonest 6-mark theme; why the brakes cannot stop the car, with an impulse calculation, has not been set.

items.question: A muon and an antimuon, both at rest, annihilate. Two gamma photons of equal energy are produced. mass of muon = 106 MeV/c² What is the frequency of each photon? 2.6 × 10¹⁶ Hz 1.3 × 10²² Hz 2.6 × 10²² Hz 5.1 × 10²² Hz
items.ms: The total rest energy is 2 × 106 MeV, shared between two photons, so each photon has 106 MeV = 106 × 10⁶ × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J = 1.70 × 10⁻¹¹ J; f = E/h = 2.56 × 10²² Hz. A leaves out the 10⁶ in MeV; B shares the rest energy of only one muon between the two photons; D gives the rest energy of both particles to one photon.
items.why: S118 has come up in 11 of 19 sessions, with annihilation-photon MCQs in Jan2025 Q7 and Jun2025 Q7; a muon–antimuon pair, with the answer as a frequency (Jun2021 Q18(d), Jan2026 Q18(d)), has not been used.

items.question: A Ξ⁻ baryon at rest decays into a Λ⁰ baryon and a π⁻ meson. mass of Ξ⁻ = 1322 MeV/c² mass of Λ⁰ = 1116 MeV/c² mass of π⁻ = 140 MeV/c² What is the total kinetic energy of the Λ⁰ and the π⁻? 66 MeV 206 MeV 1182 MeV 2578 MeV
items.ms: Energy released = (rest energy before) − (rest energy after) = 1322 − (1116 + 140) = 66 MeV, which becomes kinetic energy of the products. B subtracts the rest energy of the Λ⁰ only; C subtracts the rest energy of the π⁻ only; D adds all the rest energies.
items.why: Energy released in a decay from the change in rest mass was asked in Jun2026 Q18(c), and the Oct2021 report notes candidates 'not appreciating the need to subtract' the rest mass energy of the products.

items.question: Positron emission tomography (PET) is used in hospitals to produce images of organs inside the body. The patient is given a tracer containing a radioactive isotope that emits positrons. Each positron travels a short distance through the tissue and then annihilates with an electron. The diagram shows a cross-section through the patient and the ring of detectors around the patient. A positron and an electron annihilate at P. The two gamma photons (γ) produced are detected at the same time by detectors A and B. The positron and the electron are effectively at rest when they annihilate. Show that the energy of each gamma photon is about 0.5 MeV. Calculate the frequency of each gamma photon. Explain why the annihilation must produce two photons rather than one, and why the two photons travel in opposite directions. Some positrons annihilate before they have lost all their kinetic energy. A positron with kinetic energy 0.25 MeV annihilates with an electron at rest. Calculate the total energy, in J, of the two gamma photons. Explain why the two gamma photons do not travel in exactly opposite directions.
items.ms: Use of ΔE = c²Δm with the mass of one electron (or 2mₑ shared between two photons) Conversion between J and eV using 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ E = 0.512 MeV Use of E = hf f = 1.24 × 10²⁰ Hz The total momentum of the positron and electron before the annihilation is zero Momentum is conserved, so the total momentum of the photons must also be zero A single photon always has momentum, so one photon cannot have a total momentum of zero Two photons with momenta of equal magnitude in opposite directions have a total momentum of zero Rest energy of the two particles = 2 × 0.512 MeV (1.02 MeV) Kinetic energy added: total = 1.27 MeV E = 2.04 × 10⁻¹³ J The positron has momentum before the annihilation, so the total momentum is not zero The photons must have the same total momentum, so their momenta cannot be equal and opposite / the photons have a resultant momentum in the positron's direction of motion
items.why: S118 has come up in 11 of 19 sessions, with the annihilation photon's frequency asked in Jun2021 Q18(d) and Jan2026 Q18(d); why two photons are needed (momentum) and annihilation of a moving positron (the Oct2020 report's 'forgetting to add the initial kinetic energy') have not been asked.

Show that the mass of the tau particle is about 3.2 × 10⁻²⁷ kg. The tau is a lepton. A student says that, because the tau has a greater mass than a proton, it must be a baryon. items.name: Relativistic increase in particle lifetime
path: Unit 4 Further Mechanics, Fields and Particles
Nuclear and Particle Physics
S120 - situations in which the relativistic increase
items.question: Positive pions have a mean lifetime of 26 ns when at rest. In a laboratory, a beam of pions travels at 0.9999c. Without relativistic effects, the pions would travel on average only 7.8 m before decaying, but they are observed to travel on average about 550 m. Which statement explains this? The pions decay at a greater rate because they have a large kinetic energy. The pions travel faster than the speed of light in the laboratory. The rest mass of each pion decreases at high speed, so the pions decay more slowly. The mean lifetime of the pions, as measured in the laboratory, is much longer than 26 ns.
items.ms: At speeds close to c there is a relativistic increase in lifetime: the lifetime measured by an observer in the laboratory is much longer than 26 ns, so the pions travel much further. A: a greater rate of decay would shorten the distance. B: nothing travels faster than light. C: the rest mass does not change.
items.why: Lifetime MCQs came up in Jun2022 Q7, Jun2025 Q4 and Oct2025 Q5; a laboratory pion beam replaces the usual cosmic-ray muons, and the observer-measured lifetime is the point the digest's pitfalls stress.

S120 - situations in which the relativistic increase
items.question: The table shows the rest mass and the kinetic energy of four unstable particles. For which particle is the relativistic increase in lifetime most significant? neutron kaon muon pion
items.ms: The increase in lifetime is significant when the speed is close to c, i.e. when the kinetic energy is not small compared with the rest energy. Kinetic energy ÷ rest energy: neutron 0.005, kaon 0.12, muon 4.7, pion 0.21. Only the muon's kinetic energy is several times its rest energy (½mv² would give v ≈ 3c, which is impossible, so the muon is highly relativistic). For A, B and D the kinetic energy is a small fraction of the rest energy, so their speeds are further from c and the increase in lifetime is much smaller.
items.why: The spec asks when the lifetime increase is significant; this has been asked only through ½mv² giving a speed above c (Jun2024 Q16(a)), never as a comparison between particles.

items.question: In an experiment at CERN, positive muons were stored in a ring. The diagram shows the ring viewed from above. items.question: The table gives the charges of three quarks. Which combination could be a baryon with a charge of −1e? d d s ū d u d s d̄ d̄ s̄
items.ms: A baryon is three quarks (or three antiquarks): d d s has charge −1/3 − 1/3 − 1/3 = −1e. B has charge −1e but is a meson (a quark and an antiquark); C has charge 0; D is three antiquarks with charge +1e.

items.question: The standard quark-lepton model predicted the existence of the top quark before it was discovered. Which statement explains why? Every quark has a corresponding antiquark. A baryon must contain three different quarks. The bottom quark had been observed to decay into a top quark. There were six leptons in three generations, so by symmetry there should be six quarks.
items.ms: The model has a pair of quarks matching each pair of leptons in each generation; with six leptons known and only five quarks, symmetry required a sixth quark to pair with the bottom quark. A is true but does not predict a new quark; B is false (e.g. u u d); C is false: the top quark is heavier than the bottom quark.
items.why: The spec names the prediction of the top quark, but it has been asked only once (Jan2023 Q18(a)(i)) and never as an MCQ.

items.question: Physicists at the LHCb experiment at CERN have found evidence for a particle P, a 'pentaquark', made of four quarks and one antiquark: u u d c c̄ The table gives the charges of these quarks. items.question: The diagram shows how the quarks and leptons of the standard quark-lepton model are arranged in three generations. The charge of each particle is given as a multiple of e. The tau neutrino was not detected until 2000, many years after the tau. Suggest why physicists were confident that the tau neutrino existed before it was detected. The B⁺ meson has a charge of +1e. It contains a bottom antiquark and one quark from the first generation. Use the diagram to deduce the other quark in the B⁺ meson. A physicist measures some properties of three particles X, Y and Z, shown in the table. Scattering experiments show no evidence that X has any internal structure. Y decays into a proton and a neutral pion. Z decays into two pions. Deduce how each of the particles X, Y and Z is classified in the standard quark-lepton model, and what each is made of. Give reasons for your answers. Y decays as follows: Y → p + π⁰ Show that charge and baryon number are both conserved in this decay. Y is at rest when it decays. mass of proton = 938 MeV/c² mass of π⁰ = 135 MeV/c² Calculate the total kinetic energy, in J, of the proton and the π⁰.
items.ms: Each generation of the model contains a pair of leptons: a charged lepton and its neutrino (as well as a pair of quarks) The tau had been found in the third generation, so by the symmetry of the model there should be a tau neutrino to pair with it The bottom antiquark has charge +1/3 e (opposite to the bottom quark) The other quark must have charge +2/3 e, and the first-generation quark with this charge is the up quark IC1 X has lepton number +1 (and baryon number 0), so X is a lepton IC2 So X is a fundamental particle, not made of quarks (consistent with no internal structure) IC3 Y has baryon number +1, so Y is a baryon IC4 So Y is made of three quarks (each quark has baryon number +1/3) IC5 Z has baryon number 0 and lepton number 0, but it has mass and decays into pions, so it is not a lepton or a photon: Z is a meson IC6 So Z is made of a quark and an antiquark (baryon numbers +1/3 − 1/3 = 0) Charge: +1 → +1 + 0, so charge is conserved Baryon number: +1 → +1 + 0, so baryon number is conserved Mass difference = 1189 − (938 + 135) = 116 MeV/c² Use of ΔE = c²Δm / conversion: 116 × 10⁶ × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ Eₖ = 1.86 × 10⁻¹¹ J
items.why: S121 has come up in 18 of 19 sessions; a 6-mark answer on classifying particles (Jan2026 Q20) is likely to return in a new form, and the symmetry argument of the model, asked only once (Jan2023 Q18(a)), is applied here to the tau neutrino.

items.question: Physicists at CERN make atoms of antihydrogen. Each antihydrogen atom is made of an antiproton and a positron. The table shows some properties of the electron and the proton. Complete the table for the positron and the antiproton. The neutron has zero charge. Explain how the antineutron can be a different particle from the neutron. Suggest why antihydrogen atoms cannot be stored in a container made of ordinary matter.
items.ms: Positron: 9.11 × 10⁻³¹, +1, 0, −1 Antiproton: 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷, −1, −1, 0 The antineutron is made of antiquarks (ū d̄ d̄), whereas the neutron is made of quarks (u d d) The antineutron has baryon number −1, whereas the neutron has baryon number +1 Each antiquark has the opposite charge to its quark, so the total charge is still zero They would annihilate with the particles (electrons and protons) in the walls of the container
items.why: S122 has come up in 6 of 19 sessions, always for the positron or the antiproton (Jan2026 Q16(a), Oct2022 Q1); a neutral particle whose antiparticle is different (the antineutron) has not been asked.

items.name: Conservation of charge, baryon number and lepton number
path: Unit 4 Further Mechanics, Fields and Particles
Nuclear and Particle Physics
S123 - how to use laws of conservation of charge, ba
items.question: Which interaction is possible? n → p + e⁻ + νₑ p + p → p + n + π⁰ π⁻ + p → n + π⁰ p + p̄ → n + π⁰
items.ms: C: charge −1 + 1 → 0 + 0, baryon number 0 + 1 → 1 + 0, lepton number 0 → 0: all conserved. A: lepton number 0 → 0 + 1 + 1 = 2 (an antineutrino is needed). B: charge +2 → +1. D: baryon number 1 − 1 = 0 → 1.
items.why: S123 has come up in 14 of 19 sessions, with 'which interaction is possible' MCQs in Jun2022, Jan2023, Jun2023 and Jan2024; here each impossible option breaks a different law.

items.name: Conservation of charge, baryon number and lepton number
path: Unit 4 Further Mechanics, Fields and Particles
Nuclear and Particle Physics
S123 - how to use laws of conservation of charge, ba
items.question: A negative tau lepton can decay into a negative pion and one other particle X: τ⁻ → π⁻ + X Which of the following gives the charge, baryon number and lepton number of X? charge 0, baryon number 0, lepton number +1 charge 0, baryon number 0, lepton number −1 charge −1, baryon number 0, lepton number +1 charge 0, baryon number +1, lepton number 0
items.ms: Charge: −1 = −1 + Q, so Q = 0. Baryon number: 0 = 0 + B, so B = 0. Lepton number: the τ⁻ is a lepton (+1) and the π⁻ is a meson (0), so L = +1: X is a (tau) neutrino. B gives an antineutrino; C does not conserve charge; D does not conserve baryon or lepton number.
items.why: Identifying an unknown particle X recurs (Oct2025 Q2, Jun2026 Q13(b)); a tau decay, needing the lepton number of a third-generation lepton, has not been used.

items.name: Conservation of charge, baryon number and lepton number
path: Unit 4 Further Mechanics, Fields and Particles
Nuclear and Particle Physics

items.question: Nuclear reactors emit very large numbers of electron antineutrinos. They can be detected in a large tank of liquid that contains many hydrogen nuclei (protons). An antineutrino can interact with a proton: ν̄ₑ + p → n + X Use conservation of charge and lepton number to identify particle X. A student suggests that an electron neutrino, νₑ, could take part in the same type of interaction: νₑ + p → n + X, with X the same particle as before. Deduce whether this is possible. The proton is at rest. The kinetic energies of the products are negligible. mass of proton = 938.3 MeV/c² mass of neutron = 939.6 MeV/c² mass of electron = 0.511 MeV/c² Show that the antineutrino must have an energy of at least about 1.8 MeV for the interaction to happen.
items.ms: Charge: 0 + 1 = 0 + Q, so X has a charge of +1 (e) Lepton number: −1 + 0 = 0 + L, so X has a lepton number of −1 X is a positron (antielectron) Lepton number: +1 + 0 before but 0 + (−1) = −1 after Lepton number is not conserved, so the interaction is not possible Rest energy after − rest energy before = 939.6 + 0.511 − 938.3 = 1.81 MeV
items.why: S123 has come up in 14 of 19 sessions, often as 'identify X' (Oct2025 Q2, Jun2026 Q13(b)); the reaction used to detect reactor antineutrinos has not been used, and the neutrino/antineutrino choice is the error behind the Jun2023 MCQ distractors.

path: Unit 4 Further Mechanics, Fields and Particles
Nuclear and Particle Physics

items.question: The diagram shows some tracks in a bubble chamber. There is a uniform magnetic field directed into the page. A negative pion, π⁻, enters from the left and interacts with a stationary proton at A. Two neutral particles are produced at A: a K⁰ meson and a Λ⁰ baryon. Neutral particles leave no tracks, so their paths are shown as dotted lines. The K⁰ decays at B and the Λ⁰ decays at C. Show that charge and baryon number are both conserved in the interaction at A. The K⁰ decays at B into a positive pion and a negative pion. Write a particle equation for this decay. A student suggests that the K⁰ could instead decay into a positive pion and an electron. Deduce whether this decay is possible. The Λ⁰ decays at C into a proton and a negative pion. Explain which of the tracks labelled 1 and 2 is made by the proton.
items.ms: Charge: −1 + (+1) → 0 + 0 (values for all four particles) Total charge 0 before and 0 after, so charge is conserved Baryon number: 0 + 1 → 0 + 1 (values for all four particles) Total baryon number 1 before and 1 after, so baryon number is conserved K⁰ → π⁺ + π⁻ Lepton number: 0 → 0 + 1, so lepton number is not conserved So the decay is not possible The Λ⁰ is neutral, so the two particles have opposite charges and curve in opposite directions Fleming's left-hand rule / F = Bqv: a positive particle in a field into the page curves anticlockwise (to the left of its direction of motion) So track 1 is made by the proton Track 1 is less curved, so it has a greater momentum (r = p/BQ), as expected for the much more massive proton
items.why: S123 has come up in 14 of 19 sessions, and 'show that charge and baryon number are conserved' (Jun2026 Q13(a), Jun2025 Q14(a)(ii)) recurs; associated production in a bubble chamber has not been used, and lepton number ruling out a decay that conserves charge is the rarer angle.

items.name: Electric field as a region of force on a charge
path: Unit 4 Further Mechanics, Fields and Particles

items.question: The base of a thundercloud is negatively charged. There is an electric field between the base of the cloud and the ground. The field can be represented by electric field lines. State what is meant by an electric field. Explain why two electric field lines can never cross.
items.ms: A region where a charged particle experiences a force The direction of a field line at a point is the direction of the force on a positive charge at that point Where two lines crossed, the force on a charge would have two different directions, but the (resultant) force on a charge at a point can only have one direction
items.why: S92 was asked in 4 of 19 sessions, last as 'State what is meant by an electric field' (Jun2026 Q11(a) and Q19(a)); why field lines cannot cross follows from that definition and has never been asked.

items.question: A proton and an alpha particle are each released from rest in the same uniform electric field. What is the value of (initial acceleration of the proton) ÷ (initial acceleration of the alpha particle)? 0.25 0.50 2.0 4.0
items.ms: a = F/m = EQ/m. The proton has charge e and mass 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg; the alpha particle has charge 2e and mass 6.64 × 10⁻²⁷ kg (about 4 times as much), so its acceleration is about half as big: ratio = (1/1.67) ÷ (2/6.64) = 2.0. A uses the masses only and inverts the ratio. B inverts the ratio. D uses the masses only, ignoring the charges.
items.why: S93 was asked in only 4 of 19 sessions, last in Jan2024; Jan2023 Q10 compared a proton with a helium nucleus in the same uniform field, so a ratio of accelerations (F = EQ, then a = F/m) is a likely re-angle.

items.name: Coulomb's law: F = Q₁Q₂/4πε₀r²
path: Unit 4 Further Mechanics, Fields and Particles

items.question: Two small charged spheres are a distance d apart. The electrostatic force between them is F. The charge on one sphere is doubled and the distance between the centres of the spheres is increased to 1.5d. What is the new electrostatic force between the spheres? 0.89F 1.3F 3.0F 4.5F
items.ms: F ∝ Q₁Q₂/r², so the new force = F × 2 ÷ 1.5² = 0.89F. B does not square the distance (2 ÷ 1.5). C multiplies by the distance factor instead of dividing (2 × 1.5). D multiplies by the square of the distance factor (2 × 1.5²).
items.why: Scaling MCQs on Coulomb's law recur (Oct2020 Q8, Jun2026 Q10); a non-integer change in separation together with a change of charge tests the inverse square law properly.

items.name: Coulomb's law: F = Q₁Q₂/4πε₀r²
path: Unit 4 Further Mechanics, Fields and Particles
Electric and Magnetic Fields
S94 - use the equation F  for the force between two
items.question: Three small charged spheres X, Y and Z lie in that order on a straight line. X and Z each have a charge of +Q and Y has a charge of +q. The distance XY is d and the distance YZ is 2d. When Z is removed, the electrostatic force on Y is F. What is the magnitude of the resultant electrostatic force on Y when all three spheres are present? 0.50F 0.75F 1.25F 1.5F
items.ms: The force on Y due to Z = F × (d/2d)² = F/4. X repels Y towards Z and Z repels Y towards X, so the forces are in opposite directions: resultant = F − F/4 = 0.75F. A does not square the distance (F − F/2). C adds the forces, ignoring their directions. D adds the forces and does not square the distance.
items.why: S94 came up in 13 of 19 sessions, always for a single pair of charges; the resultant force from two charges acting along a line has not been asked.

items.name: Field of a point charge: E = Q/4πε₀r²
path: Unit 4 Further Mechanics, Fields and Particles

items.question: The electric potential at a distance of 0.20 m from a point charge is 900 V. What is the electric field strength at a distance of 0.60 m from the point charge? 500 N C⁻¹ 830 N C⁻¹ 1500 N C⁻¹ 4500 N C⁻¹
items.ms: Q/4πε₀ = Vr = 900 V × 0.20 m = 180 V m, so E = Q/4πε₀r² = 180 ÷ 0.60² = 500 N C⁻¹ (equivalently, the potential at 0.60 m is 300 V and E = V/r = 300 ÷ 0.60). B divides the potential at 0.60 m by r². C divides the potential at 0.20 m by 0.60 m. D is the field strength at 0.20 m (900 ÷ 0.20).
items.why: S95 came up in 11 of 19 sessions, mostly E = Q/4πε₀r² from a given charge (Oct2025 Q11, Jun2026 Q11(b)); linking E and V for the same point charge has not been asked.

items.name: Field of a point charge: E = Q/4πε₀r²
path: Unit 4 Further Mechanics, Fields and Particles

items.question: Two point charges, +Q and +4Q, are fixed a distance d apart. At what distance from the +Q charge, on the line between the charges, is the resultant electric field strength zero? d/5 d/3 d/2 2d/3
items.ms: The two fields are equal and opposite at the null point: Q/x² = 4Q/(d − x)², so d − x = 2x and x = d/3. A uses the ratio of the charges without the square (x/(d − x) = 1/4). C ignores the different charges. D is the distance from the +4Q charge (the null point is nearer the smaller charge).
items.why: Superposition of point-charge fields recurs (Jan2021 Q7, Jun2021 Q16(a), Oct2024 Q12(b)), and the Oct2022 MCQ on a null point shows the reverse question is set; the position is found from E = Q/4πε₀r².

items.ms: Use of V = Q/4πε₀r with a pair of values read from the graph Q = 3.0 × 10⁻⁸ C Tangent drawn to the curve at r = 0.30 m Gradient of the tangent calculated using a large triangle E = 3.0 × 10³ V m⁻¹ The field strength is equal to (minus) the potential gradient, not to the potential The gradient at 0.60 m is a quarter of the gradient at 0.30 m (E ∝ 1/r² but V ∝ 1/r), so E is about 750 V m⁻¹ and the student is not correct

items.question: An oil drop carrying a charge of 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁸ C is between two horizontal parallel plates 4.0 mm apart. The potential difference between the plates is 1.2 kV. What is the magnitude of the electric force on the drop? 9.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ N 9.6 × 10⁻¹⁶ N 3.8 × 10⁻¹⁵ N 9.6 × 10⁻¹³ N
items.ms: E = V/d = 1200 V ÷ 0.0040 m = 3.0 × 10⁵ V m⁻¹; F = EQ = 3.0 × 10⁵ × 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁸ = 9.6 × 10⁻¹³ N. A uses 1.2 V and 4.0 m (no unit conversions). B leaves the separation in mm. C uses F = QV, leaving out the separation.

items.question: A charged oil drop is held stationary between two horizontal parallel plates by the electric field between them. The polarity of the p.d. between the plates is suddenly reversed, without changing its size. What is the initial acceleration of the drop? zero 9.81 m s⁻² downwards 19.6 m s⁻² upwards 19.6 m s⁻² downwards
items.ms: Before the change, the electric force is mg upwards. After the reversal it is mg downwards, so the resultant force is 2mg downwards and a = 2g = 19.6 m s⁻² downwards. A assumes the forces still balance because the size of the p.d. has not changed. B ignores the electric force after the reversal. C has the direction of the resultant force wrong.
items.why: Balanced-drop (Millikan) set-ups recur (Jan2021 Q19, Jan2025 Q16(b)); what happens when the field is changed has not been asked.

items.question: An alpha particle is accelerated from rest from one plate to the other between two parallel plates 5.0 cm apart. The p.d. between the plates is 2.5 kV. What is the kinetic energy gained by the alpha particle? 4.0 × 10⁻¹⁷ J 4.0 × 10⁻¹⁶ J 8.0 × 10⁻¹⁶ J 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁴ J

items.question: Waste plastic flakes can be sorted by charging them and letting them fall between two vertical metal plates, as shown. Flakes of PET become positively charged and flakes of PVC become negatively charged. The flakes are released from rest at the top, midway between the plates. The plates are 1.2 m high and 0.30 m apart. The left plate is at +20 kV and the right plate is at −20 kV. Each flake has a mass of 2.0 × 10⁻⁵ kg and a charge of magnitude 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ C. Ignore air resistance. Show that a flake takes about 0.5 s to fall the height of the plates. Calculate the horizontal acceleration of a flake. The PET flakes and the PVC flakes must be at least 15 cm apart when they leave the bottom of the plates. Deduce whether this requirement is met. A student predicts that each flake follows a curved path between the plates, like a projectile. Explain why each flake moves in a straight line.
items.ms: Use of s = ut + ½at² with u = 0 and a = 9.81 m s⁻² t = 0.49 s Use of E = V/d with V = 40 kV (4.0 × 10⁴ V) Use of F = EQ and a = F/m a = 0.67 m s⁻² Use of s = ½at² for the horizontal displacement, with the time from (a) Horizontal displacement of each flake = 8.2 cm Separation = 16.3 cm, which is greater than 15 cm, so the requirement is met The flake starts from rest The electric force (horizontal) and the weight (vertical) are both constant, so the resultant force is constant in size and direction so the acceleration is constant and the velocity is always in the direction of the resultant force, so the flake moves in a straight line
items.why: Charged particles moving in a uniform field are the most common long S97 question (Oct2023 Q22, Jun2025 Q19, Jan2026 Q18(b)); a particle released from rest, whose path is straight rather than parabolic, has not been asked.

items.question: The diagram shows an electron beam tube. The tube contains a vacuum. Electrons released from the heated filament are accelerated through a p.d. of 2400 V to the anode. They pass through a hole in the anode and enter the region between two horizontal parallel plates, midway between the plates and moving parallel to them. The plates are 6.0 cm long and 2.0 cm apart. The upper plate is at a potential of +90 V and the lower plate is at −90 V. Show that the speed of the electrons as they enter the region between the plates is about 2.9 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹. Explain why the electrons follow a curved path between the plates. Consider an electron while it is between the plates. Calculate the vertical acceleration of the electron. Determine the vertical displacement of the electron when it leaves the region between the plates. A uniform magnetic field is now applied in the region between the plates, perpendicular to the plane of the diagram. The electrons now pass between the plates without being deflected. Calculate the magnetic flux density of this field and state its direction. The accelerating p.d. is now increased. Both fields between the plates are unchanged. Explain how the path of the electrons between the plates changes.
items.ms: Use of eV = ½mv² v = 2.90 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹ There is a constant resultant force on each electron in the vertical direction (towards the positive plate), so the electron accelerates vertically There is no horizontal force, so the horizontal velocity stays constant (the vertical velocity increases while the horizontal velocity does not, so the path curves) Use of E = V/d with V = 180 V and d = 0.020 m Use of F = EQ and a = F/m a = 1.58 × 10¹⁵ m s⁻² Time between the plates t = horizontal distance ÷ horizontal speed = 2.07 × 10⁻⁹ s Use of s = ut + ½at² with u = 0 s = 3.4 × 10⁻³ m Magnetic force = electric force: Bev = eE B = 3.1 × 10⁻⁴ T Into the plane of the diagram (into the page) The electrons enter with a greater speed, so the magnetic force (Bev) increases but the electric force (eE) is unchanged so there is a resultant downward force and the beam curves downwards (towards the lower plate)
items.why: S97 is the most-examined point in this topic (15 of 19 sessions), with electron deflection between plates in Oct2023 Q22, Oct2025 Q17(c) and Q21(b); adding crossed fields (the S106 velocity selector, Jan2023 Q17) and asking what a faster beam does has not been asked.

items.question: The electric potential at a distance of 0.50 m from the centre of a small positively charged sphere is 360 V. A point charge of +2.0 nC moves from a point 0.25 m from the centre of the sphere to a point 0.50 m from the centre. How much work is done on the point charge by the electric field? 7.2 × 10⁻⁷ J 1.4 × 10⁻⁶ J 2.2 × 10⁻⁶ J 2.9 × 10⁻⁶ J
items.ms: V ∝ 1/r, so the potential at 0.25 m is 720 V. W = QΔV = 2.0 × 10⁻⁹ × (720 − 360) = 7.2 × 10⁻⁷ J. B uses the potential at 0.25 m only. C takes V ∝ 1/r² (1440 V − 360 V). D uses V ∝ 1/r² and the potential at 0.25 m only.
items.why: S98 came up in 13 of 19 sessions; work done moving a charge between two radii was asked in Jan2023 Q12(c), and confusing V ∝ 1/r with E ∝ 1/r² is the usual error.

items.name: V = Q/4πε₀r for a radial field
path: Unit 4 Further Mechanics, Fields and Particles
Electric and Magnetic Fields
S98 - use V  for a radial field 4 0 r
items.question: Two point charges, +Q and −Q, are fixed a distance d apart. M is the midpoint of the line joining them. Which row describes the electric potential and the electric field strength at M? potential: zero; field strength: zero potential: non-zero; field strength: zero potential: zero; field strength: non-zero, directed towards +Q potential: zero; field strength: non-zero, directed towards −Q
items.ms: Potential is a scalar: Q/4πε₀(d/2) + (−Q)/4πε₀(d/2) = 0. Field strength is a vector: at M the field due to +Q points away from +Q and the field due to −Q points towards −Q, so the two fields are in the same direction, add, and the resultant points towards −Q. A treats the fields as cancelling like the potentials. B swaps the behaviour of the scalar and the vector. C reverses the field direction (the field direction is the direction of the force on a positive charge).
items.why: Jun2026 Q8 asked the potential at a midpoint and Jun2021 Q16(a) the field midway between opposite charges; comparing the scalar and the vector at the same point combines the two.

items.question: Alpha particles, each with a kinetic energy of 7.7 MeV, are fired at a thin aluminium foil. An aluminium nucleus is ²⁷₁₃Al. Show that the distance of closest approach of an alpha particle to an aluminium nucleus, in a head-on collision, is about 5 × 10⁻¹⁵ m. State one assumption made in your calculation in (a). The radius of an aluminium nucleus is 3.6 × 10⁻¹⁵ m and the radius of an alpha particle is 1.9 × 10⁻¹⁵ m. Deduce whether the point-charge model used in (a) is valid for this collision. In another experiment, alpha particles with the same kinetic energy are fired at a gold foil. A gold nucleus has 79 protons and a radius of 7.0 × 10⁻¹⁵ m. Determine whether these alpha particles reach the surface of a gold nucleus in a head-on collision. Calculate the minimum kinetic energy, in MeV, that an alpha particle needs to just touch an aluminium nucleus in a head-on collision.
items.ms: Conversion of 7.7 MeV to J: 1.23 × 10⁻¹² J Charges 2 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C and 13 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C used Initial kinetic energy = electric potential energy at closest approach: Ek = QαV with V = QAl/4πε₀r r = 4.86 × 10⁻¹⁵ m The aluminium nucleus does not move (recoil) The nucleus and the alpha particle act as point charges The only force on the alpha particle is the electrostatic force from the nucleus (the atom's electrons have no effect) The centres cannot be closer than 3.6 + 1.9 = 5.5 × 10⁻¹⁵ m without the particles touching 5.5 × 10⁻¹⁵ m is greater than 4.9 × 10⁻¹⁵ m, so the alpha particle would reach the nucleus and the point-charge model is not valid Closest approach ∝ charge on the nucleus (or a full recalculation with Q = 79e) r = 2.95 × 10⁻¹⁴ m This is greater than 7.0 + 1.9 = 8.9 × 10⁻¹⁵ m, so the alpha particles do not reach the gold nucleus Use of V = Q/4πε₀r with r = 5.5 × 10⁻¹⁵ m and Q = 13 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C Ek = QV with Q = 2 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C: Ek = 1.09 × 10⁻¹² J Ek = 6.8 MeV
items.why: Closest approach from E_{k} = QV with V = Q/4πε₀r is the most repeated S98 calculation (Jan2021 Q18, Jun2022 Q16, Oct2023 Q15, Oct2025 Q19); a light nucleus that the alpha particle actually reaches, so the point-charge model fails, has not been asked.

items.question: Which statement about the equipotentials around an isolated positive point charge is correct? Equipotentials at equal intervals of potential are equally spaced. Equipotentials at equal intervals of potential get further apart as the distance from the charge increases. Equipotentials are parallel to the electric field lines. items.question: The diagram shows the electric field lines around two point charges X and Y. Which row describes the charges? X: positive; Y: negative; larger magnitude of charge: X X: positive; Y: negative; larger magnitude of charge: Y X: negative; Y: positive; larger magnitude of charge: X X: negative; Y: positive; larger magnitude of charge: Y
items.ms: The arrows point away from X and into Y: field lines start on positive charges and end on negative charges. All 16 lines leave X but only 8 of them end on Y (the rest go off to a large distance), so X has the larger charge (about twice that of Y). B reads the number of lines the wrong way round. C and D reverse the field direction.
items.why: Field-line MCQs recur (Jan2023 Q6, Oct2025 Q1, Jun2026 Q6, all with charges of equal size); unequal charges, where the number of lines shows the relative size, have not been asked.

items.question: Two parallel plates are 4.8 cm apart. The p.d. between them is 240 V. Equipotentials are drawn between the plates at intervals of 60 V. What is the distance between adjacent equipotentials? 0.83 cm 0.96 cm 1.2 cm 1.6 cm
items.ms: The field between the plates is uniform: E = 240 V ÷ 4.8 cm = 50 V cm⁻¹, so a 60 V step needs 60 ÷ 50 = 1.2 cm (240 V ÷ 60 V = 4 equal gaps across 4.8 cm). A inverts the ratio (50 ÷ 60). B divides 4.8 cm by 5, the number of equipotentials including the plates. D divides by 3, the number of equipotentials between the plates.
items.why: Field lines between parallel plates are drawn in most sessions (Jan2025 Q16(a), Jun2025 Q19(a), Jun2026 Q19(a)); equally spaced equipotentials in a uniform field are the counterpart not yet asked.

items.question: A small metal sphere is held above a large earthed metal plate. The sphere is at a potential of +1000 V. The diagram shows a cross-section through the sphere and the plate, with equipotentials at 250 V intervals. X is a point directly below the centre of the sphere. Add four electric field lines to the diagram to show the electric field between the sphere and the plate. State and explain where the electric field strength is greatest. Estimate the electric field strength at X. An electron is released from rest at the point on the plate directly below the sphere. Calculate the kinetic energy of the electron when it reaches the sphere.
items.ms: Lines start on the sphere and end on the plate, meeting both surfaces at right angles Lines cross every equipotential at right angles Arrows pointing away from the sphere, towards the plate Just below the sphere (at the surface of the sphere nearest the plate) because the equipotentials are closest together there (the potential gradient is greatest) Use of E = ΔV/Δd with ΔV = 250 V and Δd read from the diagram (about 1.8 cm) E = 1.4 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹ Use of W = QV with V = 1000 V Ek = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁶ J

items.name: Impulse: F∆t = ∆p (Newton's second law)
path: Unit 4 Further Mechanics, Fields and Particles

items.question: A graph is plotted of the momentum p of an object against time t. What is represented by the gradient of the graph? the impulse on the object the kinetic energy of the object the acceleration of the object the resultant force on the object
items.ms: Resultant force = rate of change of momentum (F = Δp/Δt), so the gradient of a p–t graph is the resultant force (D). A: impulse is a change in momentum (or the area under a force–time graph), not a rate of change. B: kinetic energy is p²/2m, not a gradient. C: acceleration is the gradient of a velocity–time graph; the gradient of a p–t graph is m × a.
items.why: May 2024 Q8 asked what the area under a force–time graph represents and Oct2023 Q2 asked Δp = FΔt; the matching idea that the gradient of a momentum–time graph is the resultant force has not been asked.

items.question: A golf club strikes a stationary golf ball of mass 0.046 kg. During the contact, the force on the ball increases uniformly from zero to 5.2 kN and then decreases uniformly to zero. The contact lasts 0.50 ms. What is the speed of the ball as it leaves the club? 14 m s⁻¹ 28 m s⁻¹ 57 m s⁻¹ 280 m s⁻¹
items.ms: Impulse = area under the force–time graph = ½ × 5.2 × 10³ N × 0.50 × 10⁻³ s = 1.3 N s = Δp, so v = 1.3 ÷ 0.046 = 28 m s⁻¹ (B). A halves twice (uses the mean force ½F_max and the ½ of the triangle area). C uses F_max × t, leaving out the ½ for the triangle. D converts 0.50 ms to 5.0 × 10⁻³ s.
items.why: Impulse MCQs come up in most sessions (Oct2023, Jan2024, Oct2025, Jan2026, Jun2026); the area under a force–time graph has only been asked as a definition (May 2024 Q8), never used to find a speed.

path: Unit 4 Further Mechanics, Fields and Particles

items.question: A ball of mass m travelling at speed v strikes a smooth vertical wall. Its velocity makes an angle θ with the surface of the wall. The ball rebounds with the same speed v, also at an angle θ to the surface of the wall. What is the magnitude of the change in momentum of the ball? 0 2mv cos θ 2mv sin θ 2mv
items.ms: Only the velocity component perpendicular to the wall reverses. With θ measured from the surface of the wall this component is v sin θ, so Δp = mv sin θ − (−mv sin θ) = 2mv sin θ (C). A: the speed is unchanged but the velocity is not, so the momentum changes. B uses the component parallel to the wall, which does not change. D treats the impact as head-on.
items.why: Rebound MCQs (Jan2024 Q9, Oct2025 Q9, Jan2026 Q2) have all been head-on; an oblique rebound, where only the perpendicular component changes, is the likeliest variation and joins S81 to S83.

items.question: A firefighter aims a horizontal jet of water at a vertical wall, as shown. The water leaves the circular nozzle at a speed of 24 m s⁻¹. The diameter of the nozzle is 2.5 cm. density of water = 1000 kg m⁻³ Show that about 12 kg of water leaves the nozzle each second. The water hits the wall at 24 m s⁻¹ and then runs down the wall, so its horizontal velocity becomes zero. Calculate the horizontal force exerted on the wall by the water. Explain why the firefighter must push the nozzle forwards to keep it stationary. The firefighter changes to a nozzle of smaller diameter. The volume of water leaving the nozzle each second does not change. Explain how this change affects the force exerted on the wall.
items.ms: Use of A = πr² with r = 1.25 × 10⁻² m Use of mass per second = ρAv Mass per second = 11.8 kg (s⁻¹) Use of F = Δp/Δt, with Δp/Δt = mass per second × change in velocity F = 283 N The nozzle exerts a forward force on the water to increase its (forward) momentum By Newton's third law the water exerts an equal and opposite (backward) force on the nozzle, so a forward push is needed for the resultant force on the nozzle to be zero The water leaves the nozzle at a greater speed (the same volume per second passes through a smaller area) The mass per second is unchanged, so the rate of change of momentum at the wall, and so the force, is greater
