items.question: A spacecraft of total mass 850 kg is far from any planet or star. A small thruster on the spacecraft ejects gas backwards at a speed of 1.8 km s⁻¹ relative to the spacecraft. The thruster ejects 0.045 kg of gas each second. Show that the force exerted on the spacecraft by the thruster is about 80 N. The thruster fires for 120 s. Calculate the change in speed of the spacecraft. Assume that the mass of the spacecraft does not change. Explain how the thruster makes the spacecraft accelerate, and why the acceleration of the spacecraft increases slightly while the thruster is firing.
items.ms: Use of F = Δp/Δt (force = mass of gas ejected per second × speed of the gas) F = 81 N Use of impulse = FΔt Use of Δp = mΔv Δv = 11.4 m s⁻¹ IC1 The thruster pushes the gas backwards, so the gas gains backward momentum IC2 By Newton's third law the gas exerts an equal and opposite (forward) force on the spacecraft IC3 No external force acts on the spacecraft and gas, so the forward momentum gained by the spacecraft equals the backward momentum given to the gas IC4 The force on the spacecraft equals the rate of change of momentum of the gas (mass ejected per second × speed of the gas) IC5 The mass ejected per second and the speed of the gas are constant, so the force is constant IC6 The mass of the spacecraft decreases as gas is ejected, so the acceleration (a = F/m) increases
items.why: S81 has come up in 16 of 19 sessions and the rate of change of momentum of an ejected fluid was asked in Oct2024 Q17(a) and Jun2026 Q11; Oct2025 Q16 set a 6-mark momentum-and-impulse discussion, and thrust in space has not yet been asked.

items.name: Core Practical 9: force exerted on an object and its change of momentum
path: Unit 4 Further Mechanics, Fields and Particles
Further Mechanics
S82 - CORE PRACTICAL 9 Investigate the relationship
items.question: A student investigates the relationship between the force on an object and its rate of change of momentum, using the apparatus shown. A trolley carrying a card and a force sensor is pulled along a horizontal runway by a string that passes over a pulley to a hanging mass. The force sensor measures the force F exerted by the string on the trolley. The trolley passes through two light gates, A and B, which are connected to a data logger. mass of trolley, card and force sensor = 0.750 kg Describe how the student could use the light gates and the data logger to determine the change in momentum Δp of the trolley between A and B. The student varies F by changing the hanging mass. For each value of F the data logger gives Δp and the time Δt taken by the trolley to travel from A to B. The results are shown in the table. Complete the table. Plot a graph of Δp/Δt against F on the grid. Determine the gradient of your graph. The student concludes that the rate of change of momentum of the trolley is equal to F. Discuss whether the graph supports this conclusion.
items.ms: Measure the length of the card (with vernier calipers or a ruler) The data logger records the time for the card to pass through each light gate Speed at each gate = length of card ÷ time Δp = m(v − u), where u is the speed at A and v is the speed at B Both values correct: 0.443 N and 1.06 N (to 2 or 3 s.f.) Axes labelled with quantities and units: Δp/Δt / N and F / N Sensible scales: the plotted points cover at least half the grid in each direction All points plotted accurately (to within half a small square) Single straight line of best fit Gradient calculated using a large triangle (at least half the length of the line) Gradient = 0.99 (accept 0.95–1.05; no unit) A gradient of about 1 shows that Δp/Δt increases by the same amount as F The line does not pass through the origin: Δp/Δt is about 0.15 N less than F at every value (intercept on the F axis ≈ 0.15 N) So Δp/Δt equals the resultant force, F minus a constant frictional force; the conclusion is not correct as stated
items.why: Core Practical 9 has never been examined directly in 19 sessions (the nearest items use light gates to find momentum, e.g. Jun2022 Q18(a)); a plotted test of resultant force = rate of change of momentum, with friction as the intercept, is the likeliest form when it appears.

items.name: Momentum in two dimensions
path: Unit 4 Further Mechanics, Fields and Particles
Further Mechanics
S83 - how to apply conservation of linear momentum
items.question: On a snooker table, a ball moving due east strikes a stationary ball of equal mass. After the collision the first ball moves in a direction north of east. Which statement about the second ball immediately after the collision is correct? The southward component of its momentum is equal to the northward component of the first ball's momentum. The northward component of its momentum is equal to the northward component of the first ball's momentum. Its momentum has no component to the north or to the south. The eastward component of its momentum is equal to the momentum of the first ball before the collision.
items.ms: There is no north–south momentum before the collision, so the north–south components after it must cancel: the second ball moves south of east with a southward component equal to the first ball's northward component (A). B would give a total northward momentum of twice the first ball's component. C leaves the first ball's northward momentum unbalanced. D ignores the eastward momentum the first ball still has, so the total eastward momentum would increase.
items.why: S83 has come up in 17 of 19 sessions, and the digest's examiner-report pitfalls include conserving momentum in the wrong direction; Jun2026 Q15(a) tested the same idea in words.

items.name: Momentum in two dimensions
path: Unit 4 Further Mechanics, Fields and Particles
Further Mechanics
S83 - how to apply conservation of linear momentum
items.question: Two ice skaters collide and hold on to each other. Before the collision, skater X, of mass 60 kg, moves due east at 2.0 m s⁻¹ and skater Y, of mass 40 kg, moves due north at 4.5 m s⁻¹. What is the speed of the skaters immediately after the collision? 1.8 m s⁻¹ 2.2 m s⁻¹ 3.0 m s⁻¹ 4.9 m s⁻¹
items.ms: The momenta are perpendicular: p = √(120² + 180²) = 216 kg m s⁻¹, so v = 216 ÷ 100 = 2.2 m s⁻¹ (B). A uses only Y's momentum (180 ÷ 100). C adds the momenta as scalars (300 ÷ 100). D combines the velocities instead of the momenta: √(2.0² + 4.5²).
items.why: Bodies that join after a two-dimensional collision were asked in Jun2026 Q12 (docking) and Jan2026 Q12 (DART); it is the commonest short S83 calculation.

items.name: Momentum in two dimensions
path: Unit 4 Further Mechanics, Fields and Particles
Further Mechanics
S83 - how to apply conservation of linear momentum
items.question: A particle moving due east decays into two particles. Immediately after the decay each particle has momentum of magnitude q. One moves at 30° north of east and the other at 30° south of east. What was the magnitude of the momentum of the original particle? 0.87q 1.0q 1.7q 2.0q
items.ms: The north–south components cancel and the eastward components add: 2q cos 30° = 1.7q (C). A uses q cos 30° for one particle only. B uses 2q sin 30°, adding the components that cancel. D adds the magnitudes as if both particles moved due east.
items.why: Particle decays analysed with momentum components have appeared in Oct2020 Q17(b), May 2024 Q2 and Oct2024 Q18(b); the symmetric decay of a moving particle has not been asked.

items.name: Momentum in two dimensions
path: Unit 4 Further Mechanics, Fields and Particles
Further Mechanics
S83 - how to apply conservation of linear momentum
items.question: A car of mass 1250 kg travelling due north at 14.0 m s⁻¹ collides with a van of mass 1050 kg travelling due east. The vehicles lock together. Accident investigators find that, immediately after the collision, the vehicles moved in a direction 38° east of north. The speed limit on the road is 13.9 m s⁻¹. Deduce whether the van was travelling faster than the speed limit before the collision. Assume that momentum was conserved in the collision.
items.ms: Use of tan 38° = momentum of van ÷ momentum of car (or equal ratio of components) Speed of van = 13.0 m s⁻¹ 13.0 m s⁻¹ < 13.9 m s⁻¹, so the van was not travelling faster than the speed limit
items.why: Vehicle collisions were asked in Jan2025 Q19(b); working back from the direction of the wreckage to a speed before the collision, and comparing it with a limit, has not been asked.

items.name: Momentum in two dimensions
path: Unit 4 Further Mechanics, Fields and Particles
Further Mechanics
S83 - how to apply conservation of linear momentum
items.question: A firework shell is momentarily at rest at the top of its vertical flight when it explodes into three fragments, A, B and C. Immediately after the explosion all three fragments move horizontally. The diagram shows the view from above, with the velocities of A and B. mass of A = 0.12 kg mass of B = 0.080 kg mass of C = 0.15 kg Determine the speed and direction of fragment C immediately after the explosion, by drawing a scale vector diagram on the grid.
items.ms: Momenta of A and B calculated: 2.16 N s and 1.92 N s Scale stated; vectors for A and B drawn to scale, at right angles, tip to tail, with arrows Closing vector drawn for C so that the three momenta form a closed triangle; p_C = 2.9 N s (accept 2.8–3.0 N s), giving v_C = 19 m s⁻¹ (accept 18.7–20.0 m s⁻¹) Direction: 42° south of west (accept 40°–44° south of west, or 46°–50° west of south)
items.why: Scale vector diagrams of momentum were set in Oct2021 Q18(e), Jun2022 Q12(c) and Oct2022 Q16(b) but not since; a three-fragment explosion from rest is the closed-triangle case (Oct2020 Q17(b) used it for a recoiling nucleus).

items.name: Momentum in two dimensions
path: Unit 4 Further Mechanics, Fields and Particles
Further Mechanics
S83 - how to apply conservation of linear momentum
items.question: In tenpin bowling, a ball of mass 6.8 kg travelling at 8.5 m s⁻¹ strikes a stationary pin of mass 1.6 kg. The diagrams show the view from above, before and after the collision. After the collision the ball moves at 7.4 m s⁻¹ at 8.0° to its original direction. The pin moves at speed v at an angle θ to the ball's original direction, on the other side of it. Show that the component of the ball's momentum after the collision, perpendicular to its original direction, is about 7 kg m s⁻¹. Determine v and θ. Deduce whether the collision is elastic. The ball and the pin are in contact for 5.0 ms. Calculate the magnitude of the average force exerted on the pin by the ball. Frictional forces from the lane act on the ball and the pin during the collision. Explain why the total momentum of the ball and pin can still be treated as conserved during the collision.
items.ms: Use of p = mv Use of sin 8.0°, giving 7.00 kg m s⁻¹ Momentum of the ball before the collision = 57.8 kg m s⁻¹ Use of cos 8.0° for the ball's component along the original direction after the collision (49.8 kg m s⁻¹) Conservation of momentum along the original direction: pin's component = 8.0 kg m s⁻¹ Conservation of momentum perpendicular to the original direction: pin's component = 7.0 kg m s⁻¹, and use of Pythagoras for the pin's momentum (10.6 kg m s⁻¹) v = 6.6 m s⁻¹ θ = 41° Use of Ek = ½mv² (or Ek = p²/2m) Ek before = 246 J and total Ek after = 221 J (186 J + 35 J) 221 J < 246 J, so kinetic energy is not conserved and the collision is inelastic Use of F = Δp/Δt, with Δp = momentum of the pin after the collision F = 2.1 × 10³ N The frictional forces are very small compared with the forces between the ball and the pin They act only for the very short contact time, so their impulse (FΔt) is negligible compared with the momentum of the ball and pin
items.why: S83 has come up in 17 of 19 sessions, usually as a glancing collision with one unknown speed and angle followed by an elastic test (Oct2025 Q17, Jun2026 Q15); why external friction can be ignored during the collision (a small force for a short time) has not been asked.

items.name: Core Practical 10: ICT analysis of collisions between small spheres
path: Unit 4 Further Mechanics, Fields and Particles
Further Mechanics
S84 - CORE PRACTICAL 10 Use ICT to
items.question: A student uses ICT to analyse a collision between two steel ball bearings on a smooth, level table top. Ball bearing P is rolled towards ball bearing Q, which is stationary. After the collision both ball bearings move off at angles to P's original direction. The diagram shows the view from above, with the x and y directions used in the analysis. Describe how the student should set up and use a video camera and motion-tracking software to test whether momentum is conserved in the collision. The table shows the student's results. Deduce whether these results show that momentum was conserved in the collision.
items.ms: IC1 Camera mounted directly above the table, pointing vertically down, so that its view is perpendicular to the table (no parallax error in distances or angles) IC2 A ruler or grid of known size placed on the table in the field of view, to calibrate distances IC3 The frame rate is known, so the time between frames = 1 ÷ frame rate; a high frame rate is used IC4 The software tracks the x and y coordinates of each ball bearing frame by frame; velocity components = change in coordinate ÷ time, using frames just before and just after the collision IC5 The mass of each ball bearing is measured with a (top-pan) balance, and momentum components are calculated using p = mv IC6 The total momentum before and after the collision is compared in the x direction and in the y direction separately Use of p = mv for the components, with the masses in kg x direction: total before = 0.0176 kg m s⁻¹ and total after = 0.0176 kg m s⁻¹ y direction: P has +5.28 × 10⁻³ kg m s⁻¹ and Q has −5.28 × 10⁻³ kg m s⁻¹, so the total after is zero, as before Momentum is conserved in both directions, so the results show that momentum was conserved
items.why: CP10 has been examined once (Jan2026 Q14(a), 2 marks on measuring the angle, crediting a camera above the spheres or motion-tracking software); a full method followed by a component test of tracked data is the likeliest way it returns.

items.name: Elastic and inelastic collisions
path: Unit 4 Further Mechanics, Fields and Particles
Further Mechanics
S85 - how to determine whether a collision is elast
items.question: Two trolleys are at rest on a horizontal runway with a compressed spring held between them. The spring is released and the trolleys move apart in opposite directions. Which row describes the total momentum and the total kinetic energy of the trolleys after they separate, compared with before the spring is released? total momentum: unchanged; total kinetic energy: increased total momentum: unchanged; total kinetic energy: unchanged total momentum: increased; total kinetic energy: increased total momentum: increased; total kinetic energy: unchanged
items.ms: No resultant external force acts, so the total momentum stays zero (the trolleys have equal and opposite momenta). Elastic potential energy in the spring becomes kinetic energy, so the total kinetic energy increases from zero (A). B: the trolleys start at rest and end up moving, so Ek cannot be unchanged. C and D treat momentum as a scalar; the two momenta are in opposite directions and add to zero.
items.why: Momentum and kinetic-energy table MCQs recur (Oct2021 Q2, Jan2022 Q4, Oct2024 Q7, Jun2026 Q4) but have all been collisions; an 'explosion', where kinetic energy increases, has not been asked.

items.name: Elastic and inelastic collisions
path: Unit 4 Further Mechanics, Fields and Particles
Further Mechanics
S85 - how to determine whether a collision is elast
items.question: Ball X, of mass 2.0 kg, moving at 3.0 m s⁻¹ collides head-on with a stationary ball Y of mass 1.0 kg. After the collision both balls move in the original direction of X. Which pair of velocities after the collision would make the collision elastic? X: 2.0 m s⁻¹; Y: 2.0 m s⁻¹ X: 1.5 m s⁻¹; Y: 3.0 m s⁻¹ X: 1.0 m s⁻¹; Y: 4.0 m s⁻¹ X: 0.50 m s⁻¹; Y: 5.0 m s⁻¹
items.ms: All four pairs conserve momentum (6.0 kg m s⁻¹), so the test is kinetic energy: before = ½ × 2.0 × 3.0² = 9.0 J. C gives 1.0 J + 8.0 J = 9.0 J, so it is elastic. A gives 6.0 J (the balls move together: inelastic). B gives 6.75 J (inelastic). D gives 12.75 J, more than before, which is impossible without an energy source.
items.why: Nearly every S85 question is an Ek-before-and-after test (Jun2021 Q7, Oct2025 Q17(b), Jun2026 Q15(c)); here every option conserves momentum, so only the energy test finds the key.

items.name: Elastic and inelastic collisions
path: Unit 4 Further Mechanics, Fields and Particles
Further Mechanics
S85 - how to determine whether a collision is elast
items.question: Two trolleys, A and B, are on a horizontal track. Each carries a magnet, arranged so that the trolleys repel each other; the trolleys do not touch. Trolley A, of mass 0.60 kg, moves towards trolley B, of mass 0.90 kg, which is stationary. Motion sensors connected to a data logger record the velocity of each trolley. The graph shows the results. Velocities in A's original direction of motion are positive. Deduce, using the graph, whether the collision is elastic. At one instant during the interaction, both trolleys have the same velocity. Calculate the total kinetic energy of the trolleys at this instant. Explain why the total kinetic energy at this instant is less than the total kinetic energy before the interaction.
items.ms: Velocities read from the graph: A 0.50 m s⁻¹ before; A −0.10 m s⁻¹ and B 0.40 m s⁻¹ after Use of Ek = ½mv² Total Ek before = 0.075 J and total Ek after = 0.075 J (0.003 J + 0.072 J) Total Ek before = total Ek after, so the collision is elastic Common velocity = 0.20 m s⁻¹ (read from where the graphs cross) Ek = 0.030 J As the trolleys approach, work is done against the repulsive magnetic force So kinetic energy is transferred to (magnetic) potential energy stored between the magnets
items.why: S85 has come up in 10 of 19 sessions, always as an Ek-before-and-after test (Oct2025 Q17(b), Jun2026 Q15(c)); reading the velocities from data-logger graphs, and why kinetic energy dips during an elastic interaction, have not been asked.

items.name: Kinetic energy of a non-relativistic particle: Ek = p²/2m
path: Unit 4 Further Mechanics, Fields and Particles
Further Mechanics
S86 - derive and use the equation E k  for the kine
items.question: An electron and a proton have the same kinetic energy. Neither is moving at a relativistic speed. What is the value of (momentum of the electron) ÷ (momentum of the proton)? 5.4 × 10⁻⁴ 2.3 × 10⁻² 43 1.8 × 10³
items.ms: p = √(2mEk), so with equal Ek the ratio is √(m_e/m_p) = √(9.11 × 10⁻³¹ ÷ 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷) = 2.3 × 10⁻² (B). A is m_e/m_p without the square root. C is the inverse ratio √(m_p/m_e). D is m_p/m_e.
items.why: Ratio MCQs on Ek = p²/2m come up almost every year (Jun2025 Q9, Oct2025 Q3, Jan2026 Q5); an electron–proton comparison uses the data-sheet masses.

items.name: Kinetic energy of a non-relativistic particle: Ek = p²/2m
path: Unit 4 Further Mechanics, Fields and Particles
Further Mechanics
S86 - derive and use the equation E k  for the kine
items.question: An alpha particle has a kinetic energy of 5.0 MeV. What is the momentum of the alpha particle? 1.0 × 10⁻²² N s 5.2 × 10⁻²⁰ N s 7.3 × 10⁻²⁰ N s 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁹ N s
items.ms: Ek = 5.0 × 10⁶ × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J = 8.0 × 10⁻¹³ J, and p = √(2mEk) = √(2 × 6.64 × 10⁻²⁷ × 8.0 × 10⁻¹³) = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁹ N s (D). A leaves out the 10⁶ for MeV. B uses the proton mass. C leaves out the factor 2 (p = √(mEk)).
items.why: Oct2024 Q6 asked for p from Ek, and the Oct2023 examiner report flags the MeV conversion; an alpha particle with its energy in MeV combines both.

items.name: Kinetic energy of a non-relativistic particle: Ek = p²/2m
path: Unit 4 Further Mechanics, Fields and Particles
Further Mechanics
S86 - derive and use the equation E k  for the kine
items.question: A proton and an alpha particle each have a kinetic energy of 3.2 MeV. Neither is moving at a relativistic speed. Show that the kinetic energy Ek of a non-relativistic particle of mass m and momentum p is given by Ek = p²/2m The proton and the alpha particle enter the same uniform magnetic field, moving at right angles to the field. A student says that the two particles will move in circles of very different radii. Deduce whether the student is correct.
items.ms: Ek = ½mv² and p = mv, so v = p/m Substitution shown: Ek = ½m(p/m)² = p²/2m Use of p = √(2mEk) (or p ∝ √m for the same Ek) p_α ÷ p_p = 2.0 (p_p = 4.1 × 10⁻²⁰ N s and p_α = 8.2 × 10⁻²⁰ N s) Use of r = p/BQ with the charge of the alpha particle = 2e r_α ÷ r_p = 0.997 ≈ 1, so the radii are (almost) the same and the student is not correct
items.why: S86 has come up in 14 of 19 sessions, often chained with r = p/BQ (Oct2020, Jan2021, Jun2023, Jan2024); the derivation the spec asks for has never been set, and equal-energy protons and alpha particles have not been compared.

items.name: Angular displacement in radians and degrees
path: Unit 4 Further Mechanics, Fields and Particles
Further Mechanics
S87 - express angular displacement
items.question: A car park barrier has a straight, rigid arm of length 3.80 m. The arm rotates about a pivot at one end. When a car arrives, the arm rotates upwards from the horizontal through an angle of 85° and then stops. Show that the angular displacement of the arm is about 1.5 rad. Later the arm rotates downwards from the raised position. A fault stops the arm when the tip of the arm has moved a distance of 4.6 m along its arc. Calculate the angle through which the arm has turned. Give your answer in degrees.
items.ms: Use of angle in rad = angle in degrees × 2π/360 (or × π/180) θ = 1.48 rad Use of θ = s/r (θ = 1.21 rad) θ = 69.4°
items.why: S87 has appeared in 3 of 19 sessions, always as a one-step conversion (40° to radians in Jan2025, 2.3 rad to degrees in Jun2026); turning an arc length back into degrees has not yet been asked.

items.name: Angular velocity: v = ωr and T = 2π/ω
path: Unit 4 Further Mechanics, Fields and Particles
Further Mechanics
S88 - what is meant by angular velocity and be able
items.question: The disk in a computer hard drive rotates at 7200 revolutions per minute. What is the angular velocity of the disk? 19 rad s⁻¹ 120 rad s⁻¹ 754 rad s⁻¹ 4.5 × 10⁴ rad s⁻¹
items.ms: ω = 2πf = 2π × (7200 ÷ 60) s⁻¹ = 754 rad s⁻¹, so C. A divides the revolutions per second by 2π instead of multiplying; B is the number of revolutions per second, not radians per second; D multiplies by 2π but does not convert minutes to seconds.
items.why: Converting revolutions per minute to rad s⁻¹ was set in Jan2023 (centrifuge MCQ), Jun2024 and Jan2025 (washing drum); converting minutes to seconds before using 2π is the step the mark schemes test.

items.name: Angular velocity: v = ωr and T = 2π/ω
path: Unit 4 Further Mechanics, Fields and Particles
Further Mechanics
S88 - what is meant by angular velocity and be able
items.question: The blades of a wind turbine rotate with a constant angular velocity of 1.2 rad s⁻¹. How long does a blade take to turn through 120°? 0.87 s 1.7 s 5.2 s 100 s
items.ms: 120° = 2π/3 rad = 2.09 rad; t = θ/ω = 2.09 ÷ 1.2 = 1.7 s, so B. A converts 120° to π/3 rad instead of 2π/3 rad; C is the time for a whole revolution (2π/ω); D divides the angle in degrees by an angular velocity in rad s⁻¹.
items.why: Time for part of a revolution was examined in Jan2023 Q13(a)(ii) and Jan2026 Q12(b), and degree–radian slips are a recurring examiner-report error.

items.name: Angular velocity: v = ωr and T = 2π/ω
path: Unit 4 Further Mechanics, Fields and Particles
Further Mechanics
S88 - what is meant by angular velocity and be able
items.question: The Earth rotates once about its axis every 23.9 hours. The diagram shows a city C at latitude 52°. As the Earth rotates, C moves in a horizontal circle about the Earth's axis. radius of the Earth = 6.37 × 10⁶ m State what is meant by angular velocity. Show that the angular velocity of the Earth is about 7 × 10⁻⁵ rad s⁻¹. Calculate the speed of C due to the Earth's rotation.
items.ms: The angle (in radians) turned through per unit time / the rate of change of angular displacement Use of ω = 2π/T with T in seconds (T = 23.9 × 3600 s = 8.60 × 10⁴ s) ω = 7.30 × 10⁻⁵ rad s⁻¹ Radius of the circular path r = 6.37 × 10⁶ m × cos 52° (= 3.92 × 10⁶ m) Use of v = ωr v = 286 m s⁻¹
items.why: S88 has come up in 11 of 19 sessions, usually as ω = 2π/T followed by v = ωr (Oct2023 Q11, Jan2026 Q12); the meaning of angular velocity (Jun2025 Q15(a)) and a radius that must be found by geometry are the less-practised angles.

items.name: Vector diagrams: derive a = v²/r = rω²
path: Unit 4 Further Mechanics, Fields and Particles
Further Mechanics
S89 - use vector diagrams to derive the equations f
items.question: An object moves in a horizontal circle at a constant speed v. What is the magnitude of the change in its velocity as it moves through a quarter of a revolution? 0 √2 v πv/2 2v
items.ms: The initial and final velocities have the same magnitude v and are at 90° to each other. Δv = v_final − v_initial, which forms a right-angled triangle, so |Δv| = √(v² + v²) = √2 v: B. A: the speed is unchanged but the direction, and so the velocity, has changed. C uses Δv = vΔθ with Δθ = π/2, but that approximation only holds for a small angle. D is the change for half a revolution.
items.why: The velocity-change vector diagram was an MCQ in Jun2025 and Oct2025; a large-angle change, where the small-angle step Δv = vΔθ of the derivation fails, has not been asked.

items.name: Vector diagrams: derive a = v²/r = rω²
path: Unit 4 Further Mechanics, Fields and Particles
Further Mechanics
S89 - use vector diagrams to derive the equations f
items.question: Astronauts are trained in a centrifuge. An astronaut sits in a capsule at the end of a horizontal arm. The arm rotates about a vertical axis at a constant rate, so the capsule moves at a constant speed v in a horizontal circle of radius r. Explain why the astronaut is accelerating even though the speed of the capsule is constant. The diagram shows the capsule at two positions P and Q on its circular path, a short time Δt apart. In this time the radius turns through a small angle Δθ. Derive the equation a = v²/r for the centripetal acceleration of the capsule. Include a vector diagram in your answer. The centre of the capsule is 7.8 m from the axis. During one test the centripetal acceleration of the astronaut is 6.0g, where g = 9.81 m s⁻². Calculate the number of revolutions the arm makes each minute.
items.ms: Velocity is a vector (quantity) The direction of motion is continually changing, so the velocity is changing Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity Vector diagram: velocities at P and Q drawn with equal lengths and the angle Δθ between them, with Δv completing the triangle (v_Q = v_P + Δv) Δθ is small, so Δv = vΔθ (arc ≈ chord, or sin Δθ ≈ Δθ) Δθ = ωΔt and v = rω (or Δθ = vΔt/r) a = Δv/Δt = vΔθ/Δt = vω = v²/r Use of a = rω² (ω = 2.75 rad s⁻¹) Use of ω = 2π/T or f = ω/2π (T = 2.29 s) 26.2 revolutions per minute
items.why: The a = v²/r derivation has been a 4–5 mark question in five sessions, most recently Jan2026 Q19(a), and an angular velocity from a required acceleration (Jan2025 Q15(a)) is the usual follow-on; why constant speed still means acceleration is rarely asked directly.

items.name: A resultant (centripetal) force is needed for circular motion
path: Unit 4 Further Mechanics, Fields and Particles
Further Mechanics
S90 - that a resultant force (centripetal force) is
items.question: A car travels round a roundabout at a constant speed. Which statement about the car is correct? Its velocity is constant and the resultant force on it is zero. Its velocity is constant and the resultant force on it acts towards the centre of the roundabout. Its velocity is changing and the resultant force on it acts away from the centre of the roundabout. Its velocity is changing and the resultant force on it acts towards the centre of the roundabout.
items.ms: The direction of motion changes, so the velocity changes and the car accelerates towards the centre; by F = ma the resultant force also acts towards the centre: D. A and B confuse constant speed with constant velocity (and A would mean straight-line motion). C describes a 'centrifugal' force; there is no outward resultant force.
items.why: S90 is asked in 8 of 19 sessions; Oct2023 Q14 and its examiner report show candidates still invent an outward 'centrifugal' force or confuse constant speed with constant velocity.

items.name: A resultant (centripetal) force is needed for circular motion
path: Unit 4 Further Mechanics, Fields and Particles
Further Mechanics
S90 - that a resultant force (centripetal force) is
items.question: A small ball on a string is whirled in a vertical circle. At the top of the circle the ball has the minimum speed needed to stay on its circular path. Which statement about the ball at the top of the circle is correct? The tension in the string is zero and the weight of the ball provides the centripetal force. The tension in the string is equal to the weight of the ball. The resultant force on the ball is zero. An outward force on the ball balances its weight.
items.ms: At the top, weight + tension = mv²/r. The speed is least when the tension is zero, so mg = mv²/r: A. B would make the resultant force 2mg, which needs a greater speed. C: the ball is accelerating towards the centre, so the resultant force is not zero. D: there is no outward force and the ball is not in equilibrium.
items.why: Oct2025 Q16(b) asked why there is a minimum speed at the top of a vertical circle (reaction or tension zero, mg = mv²/r) and Jan2026 set a vertical-circle tension MCQ.

items.name: A resultant (centripetal) force is needed for circular motion
path: Unit 4 Further Mechanics, Fields and Particles
Further Mechanics
S90 - that a resultant force (centripetal force) is
items.question: A train travels round a bend at a constant speed of 24 m s⁻¹. The bend is an arc of a circle of radius 650 m. A passenger standing in the train holds on to a handrail. She says, "As the train goes round the bend, a force pushes me towards the outside of the bend." Explain why her statement is incorrect. One carriage has a mass of 3.6 × 10⁴ kg. On a level section of the bend, the horizontal force needed is provided by the outer rail pushing sideways on the flanges of the wheels. Calculate this force. On many bends the track is canted: the outer rail is higher than the inner rail, as shown in the diagram. Explain how canting the track reduces the sideways force that the rails must exert on the wheel flanges.
items.ms: Without a resultant force she would continue to move in a straight line / at a tangent to the bend (Newton's first law) To move in a circle there must be a resultant (centripetal) force on her towards the centre of the circle This force is provided by the handrail (and the floor) pushing or pulling her towards the centre There is no outward force: the train turns inwards relative to her straight-line path, so she only appears to move outwards relative to the train Use of F = mv²/r F = 3.19 × 10⁴ N The (normal) contact force from the track acts perpendicular to the track So the contact force has a horizontal component towards the centre of the circle This component provides some (or all) of the centripetal force, so a smaller sideways force from the rails is needed At one particular speed the horizontal component provides all of the centripetal force and no sideways force is needed
items.why: Oct2023 Q14 asked candidates to assess a passenger's 'outward force' claim and Jan2020 and Jan2026 asked about the benefit of banking; rail cant and flange forces are a fresh setting for both ideas.

items.name: A resultant (centripetal) force is needed for circular motion
path: Unit 4 Further Mechanics, Fields and Particles
Further Mechanics
S90 - that a resultant force (centripetal force) is
items.question: An aerobatic aircraft flies at a constant speed of 75 m s⁻¹ in a vertical circle of radius 320 m. The diagram shows the circle. X is the highest point and Y is the lowest point. The pilot has a mass of 72 kg. Explain why the force exerted by the seat on the pilot is greater at Y than at X. Calculate the force exerted by the seat on the pilot at Y. On a later loop of the same radius, the pilot reduces the speed at X until the seat exerts no force on the pilot at X. Calculate the speed of the aircraft at X.
items.ms: IC1 The pilot moves in a circle, so there must be a resultant (centripetal) force on the pilot towards the centre of the circle IC2 The centripetal force = mv²/r, which is the same at X and Y because v and r are constant IC3 At X and Y the only forces on the pilot are the weight and the force from the seat (both vertical) IC4 At Y the centre is above the pilot: the seat force acts upwards and the weight downwards, so seat force − weight = mv²/r IC5 At X the centre is below the pilot: the seat force and the weight both act downwards, so seat force + weight = mv²/r IC6 So the seat force is mv²/r + mg at Y and mv²/r − mg at X: it is greater at Y by 2mg Use of F = mv²/r Seat force R = mg + mv²/r (R − mg = mv²/r) R = 1.97 × 10³ N Weight alone provides the centripetal force: mg = mv²/r v = 56.0 m s⁻¹
items.why: Vertical-circle reasoning has appeared in Jan2022, Jun2023 (a 6-mark explanation), Jan2025, Oct2025 and Jan2026; the seat force on a pilot is an unasked context for the same top-and-bottom comparison.

items.name: Centripetal force and acceleration
path: Unit 4 Further Mechanics, Fields and Particles
Further Mechanics

items.question: A car of mass 1100 kg travels at a constant speed of 18 m s⁻¹ round a bend. The bend is part of a circle of diameter 120 m. What is the resultant force on the car? 330 N 3.0 × 10³ N 5.9 × 10³ N 1.7 × 10⁴ N
items.ms: F = mv²/r with r = 120 ÷ 2 = 60 m: F = 1100 × 18² ÷ 60 = 5940 N, so C. A uses mv/r; B uses the diameter as the radius; D adds the weight, which acts vertically and is balanced by the normal reaction.
items.why: S91 is the most-asked point in the topic (15 of 19 sessions), and using the diameter instead of the radius is the error the examiner reports quote most.

items.question: A space station is a large wheel that rotates at a constant angular velocity. At the rim, 120 m from the centre, the centripetal acceleration is 9.81 m s⁻². What is the centripetal acceleration at a point on a spoke, 30 m from the centre? 2.5 m s⁻² 9.8 m s⁻² 39 m s⁻² 157 m s⁻²
items.ms: Every point has the same ω, so a = rω² is proportional to r: a = 9.81 × 30/120 = 2.5 m s⁻², so A. B assumes the acceleration is the same everywhere; C uses a = v²/r as if v were the same at both radii (but v = rω is smaller nearer the centre); D treats a as proportional to 1/r².

items.question: The diagram shows a fairground swing ride. Each chair hangs from a chain of length 6.0 m attached to the edge of a horizontal canopy of radius 4.5 m. The canopy rotates about the central tower. When the ride rotates at a constant rate, each chain makes an angle of 40° with the vertical. The diagram below shows one chair and its rider, treated as a single object. Add labelled arrows to the diagram to show the forces acting on the chair and rider. Show that the angular velocity ω of the ride is given by ω² = g tan θ / r where θ is the angle between the chain and the vertical and r is the radius of the circle in which the chair moves. Calculate the time taken for one revolution of the ride. An adult and a child ride in two of the chairs. The child says, "The adult's chair will swing out further than mine because the adult is heavier." Explain whether the child is correct.
items.ms: Weight / W / mg acting vertically downwards Tension / T acting along the chain, away from the chair Resolves vertically: T cos θ = mg Resolves horizontally: T sin θ = mrω² Divides to eliminate T: tan θ = rω²/g, so ω² = g tan θ / r r = 4.5 m + 6.0 m × sin 40° (= 8.36 m) Use of ω² = g tan θ / r (ω = 0.99 rad s⁻¹) Use of T = 2π/ω T = 6.33 s The vertical component of the tension balances mg and the horizontal component provides mrω²: both are proportional to the mass So the mass cancels: tan θ = rω²/g does not depend on m All the chairs rotate with the same ω, and r depends only on θ, so both chains make the same angle and the child is incorrect
items.why: Resolving a tension to get tan θ = v²/rg came up in Jan2020, Oct2020, Oct2021, Jan2023 and Oct2024; a swing ride with r = d + L sin θ adds the geometry step the Jun2024 report says candidates get wrong, and the mass-independence argument echoes Jun2025 Q15(b).

items.question: A student investigates circular motion with the apparatus shown. A rubber bung of mass m is tied to one end of a nylon thread. The thread passes through a smooth glass tube, and a hanger with slotted masses, of total mass M = 0.150 kg, hangs from the other end. The student whirls the bung in a horizontal circle of radius r. She keeps a paper clip marker just below the tube so that r stays constant and the hanger stays at rest. Assume that the thread between the tube and the bung is horizontal. Explain why the centripetal force on the bung is equal to the weight of the hanger and slotted masses. The period of the bung's motion is T. Show that T² = (4π²m / Mg) r The student times 20 revolutions for each radius. Her results are shown in the table. Complete the table. Plot a graph of T² against r on the grid. Use your graph to determine the mass m of the bung. The student repeats the experiment with a total hanging mass of 0.300 kg. Explain how the gradient of her new graph compares with the gradient of the first graph.
items.ms: The hanger is at rest (in equilibrium), so the tension in the thread equals Mg The tension is the same throughout the thread (smooth tube), and the thread pulls the bung towards the centre of the circle, so the tension provides the centripetal force Mg = mrω² (or Mg = mv²/r) Use of ω = 2π/T (or v = 2πr/T) and rearranges to T² = 4π²mr/(Mg) T² values correct to 3 s.f.: 0.228, 0.296, 0.379, 0.448, 0.531, 0.597 Axes labelled with quantities and units: T² / s² and r / m Sensible scales, so that the plotted points cover at least half of the grid in each direction All points plotted accurately (to within half a small square) Best-fit straight line drawn Gradient calculated using a large triangle (gradient ≈ 0.75 s² m⁻¹) Use of gradient = 4π²m/(Mg) m = 0.028 kg Gradient = 4π²m/(Mg), so the gradient is inversely proportional to M M is doubled, so the gradient halves (to about 0.37 s² m⁻¹)
items.why: No WPH14 paper in the 19 sessions has set an experiment that tests F = mrω², yet Unit 4 papers regularly ask candidates to process data and plot graphs; the whirling-bung method is the standard school test of the centripetal force equation.

items.question: A student uses the circuit shown to determine the capacitance of a capacitor X. The battery has an e.m.f. of 6.00 V and negligible internal resistance. The voltmeter has a very high resistance. Capacitor X is initially uncharged. With the switch at P, the 100 μF capacitor is fully charged. The switch is then moved to Q. The voltmeter reading falls from 6.00 V to a steady value of 2.15 V. Explain why the voltmeter reading decreases when the switch is moved to Q. Determine the capacitance of X.
items.ms: Charge flows from the 100 μF capacitor to capacitor X (there is a current between the capacitors) The charge on the 100 μF capacitor decreases and V = Q/C, so the p.d. across it decreases Charge flows until the p.d. across X is equal to the p.d. across the 100 μF capacitor Use of Q = CV: initial charge = 100 × 10⁻⁶ F × 6.00 V = 6.00 × 10⁻⁴ C Charge on X = 6.00 × 10⁻⁴ C − (100 × 10⁻⁶ F × 2.15 V) = 3.85 × 10⁻⁴ C (total charge is conserved) C = 3.85 × 10⁻⁴ C ÷ 2.15 V = 1.79 × 10⁻⁴ F
items.why: S100 came up in 11 of 19 sessions; charge moving between capacitors has only been asked as a 2-mark explanation (Jan2026 Q19(c), Jan2025 Q20(d)), so using conservation of charge to find an unknown capacitance is a likely next step.

Calculate the energy transferred from the supercapacitor while the motor is turning.
items.ms: V is proportional to Q, so the graph is a straight line through the origin The work done to add a small charge ΔQ at p.d. V is VΔQ, which is the area of a thin strip under the graph So the energy stored (work done) is the total area under the graph Area of the triangle = ½ × Q × V, so W = ½QV Use of W = ½CV² Energy transferred = ½ × 47 F × (2.7² − 1.2²) V² (the difference of the two stored energies) Energy transferred = 137 J

items.question: An uncharged capacitor is connected in series with a resistor, a switch and a battery. The switch is closed and the capacitor charges. Which graph shows how the charge Q on the capacitor varies with the p.d. VR across the resistor? A B C D
items.ms: VC + VR = V₀ (the battery e.m.f.), so Q = CVC = C(V₀ − VR): a straight line with gradient −C. Q is zero when VR = V₀ (at the start) and CV₀ when VR = 0. A is the graph of Q against VC. B and C are the shapes of graphs against time (Q rising, VR falling), not against VR.
items.why: S102 graph MCQs recur (Jun2026 Q7 asked for V_{R} against t); a graph that combines V_{C} + V_{R} = V₀ with Q = CV and has no time axis has not been asked.

items.question: A capacitor is charged through a resistor of resistance R from a battery. Which change would halve the time constant of the circuit? connecting a second resistor of resistance R in parallel with the first connecting a second resistor of resistance R in series with the first using a battery with half the e.m.f. using a battery with twice the e.m.f.

V across the capacitor varies with time t for the first 100 s after the door is closed. Explain why the p.d. across the capacitor decreases in the way shown by your graph.

items.question: A student carries out an experiment to determine the capacitance C of a capacitor marked 220 μF ± 10%. The diagram shows the circuit. The battery has an e.m.f. of 6.00 V and negligible internal resistance. With the switch at X the capacitor charges. With the switch at Y the capacitor discharges through the 10.0 kΩ resistor. The student uses a data logger to record the p.d. across the capacitor, rather than a voltmeter and a stopwatch. Explain why. The student charges the capacitor and then moves the switch to Y. The table shows the p.d. V across the capacitor at time t after the switch is moved to Y. Plot a graph of ln (V / V) against t on the grid. Use the additional column of the table for your processed data. Determine C using your graph. Deduce whether the capacitor is within its stated tolerance.
items.ms: The time constant is only about 2 s (RC = 10.0 kΩ × 220 μF = 2.2 s), so the p.d. changes rapidly and the discharge is over in a few seconds A data logger can take many readings at short, precisely timed intervals (a high sampling rate) With a stopwatch, the reaction time would be significant compared with the time between readings (V and t could not be read at the same instant) ln (V / V) values correct to at least 2 d.p. Axes labelled with quantities and units, and sensible scales (points cover at least half the grid) All points plotted accurately (to within half a small square) Single straight line of best fit Gradient determined from the line using a large triangle Gradient = −1/RC (from ln V = ln V₀ − t/RC) Use of R = 10.0 kΩ to find C C = 2.26 × 10⁻⁴ F Range for 220 μF ± 10% is 198 μF to 242 μF (or the percentage difference from 220 μF is calculated) Comparison and consistent conclusion, e.g. 226 μF is between 198 μF and 242 μF, so the capacitor is within tolerance

Calculate the average power output of the flash tube while it conducts.
items.ms: Time constant RC = 2.2 × 10³ Ω × 150 × 10⁻⁶ F = 0.33 s Use of V = V₀(1 − e−t/RC) with V = 300 V and V₀ = 330 V (or the p.d. across the resistor: 30 V = 330 V × e−t/RC) t = 0.79 s 0.79 s < 1 s, so the claim is correct Curve starting on the I axis and decreasing with a decreasing gradient, not reaching or crossing the t axis Initial current marked as 0.15 A Use of W = ½CV² W = ½ × 150 × 10⁻⁶ F × (330 V)² = 8.17 J RC = 2.0 Ω × 150 × 10⁻⁶ F = 3.0 × 10⁻⁴ s Use of V = V₀e−t/RC with V = 50 V and V₀ = 330 V t = 5.7 × 10⁻⁴ s Energy remaining at 50 V = ½ × 150 × 10⁻⁶ F × (50 V)² = 0.19 J Use of P = W/t with W = 8.17 J − 0.19 J = 7.98 J P = 1.4 × 10⁴ W
